title_en: Charter, Art. 1 — The right to self-determination (part 1)
text:
Charter, Art. 1 — The right to self-determination

Older adults have the right to make independent, free, informed, and conscious decisions regarding their life choices and major decisions that affect them.

In general, older adults come from a past that did not favor the full development of their education and training, with rare exceptions. Furthermore, over the years, technological development has objectively created, with its rapid pace, difficulties in adaptation and integration. These difficulties create a gap that is also cognitive in nature, exacerbated by ageist prejudices that lead to communicating with older adults in a dismissive manner.

How to Relate to an Older Adult

This is not merely a formal principle, but a necessity for a personal and respectful approach. Re-

Interacting with an older person means adapting to their pace, their sensory and cognitive abilities, and their emotional experience, to allow for communication that is truly respectful and not frustrating for either party.

Different Paces and Slowing Down

With age, the speed of information processing, sustained attention, and, often, word retrieval slow down, even in the absence of dementia. This does not mean “less intelligence,” but rather a need for more time to understand, organize a response, and find the right words.

I ask a complex question (“What do you think, , about how the party was organized yesterday, with all those relatives?”) and after a few seconds I press with another one, frustrated that the other person “isn’t answering me.” The older person withdraws because

they feel they’re being tested.

I ask, “Do you want to go for a walk after lunch, so we can stop by the pharmacy afterward?” and I get irritated if they don’t answer right away; in reality, they’re just processing information, schedules, and their physical condition.

Hearing, vision, and environment

Presbycusis is common and often underdiagnosed: the elderly person hears the voice, but cannot distinguish

the words clearly, especially in the presence of background noise. This effort to decode speech can worsen fatigue, attention, and even social participation, leading to isolation.

Language, memory, and concentration

Aging, and even more so any forms of cognitive decline or aphasia, can make it harder to find the right words, follow abstract conversations, or switch topics abruptly. Working memory (keeping multiple elements “in mind”) and the ability to maintain concentration during long conversations may also be impaired.

The Emotional Dimension and Respect

Many older adults experience the loss of independence, social role, and health as a wound to their identity; communication can be perceived as judgment, control, or infantilization. Directive language (“You must…,” “Don’t do…”) can trigger reactions of opposition, sadness, or withdrawal.

“I’ve told you a thousand times not to get up from the bed by yourself!” conveys reproach and a sense of helplessness; a more respectful way to put it might be: “I’m worried you might fall if you get up by yourself. If you want to get up, let’s do it together—that way you’ll be safer.”

Constantly correcting (“No, that’s not how it happened…”, “You don’t remember correctly”) can be humiliating; sometimes it is more helpful to focus on the emotional experience rather than the accuracy of the content.

It is the duty of family members and those who interact with the elderly person to provide them, in light of their physical and cognitive condition, with all the information and knowledge necessary for free, full, and informed self-determination.

What to disclose

The elderly person has the right to receive information appropriate to their condition in order to make free and informed decisions; this is perfectly in line with the principle of self-determination and the rules on informed consent, which are not suspended

“simply because they are elderly,” but must be adapted to their condition.

Ethical and legal content of the duty to inform

This wording directly addresses the core of informed consent: every adult, and therefore also the elderly person, has the right to be informed in a comprehensive, understandable, and pro-

to their situation, so they can choose whether or not to accept proposed treatments or interventions that concern them. The doctrine on consent for the elderly emphasizes that their age does not justify an automatic reduction in the information provided; if anything, it requires greater care in making it accessible and in supporting their ability to exercise consent (including through tools such as supportive administration).

“In light of their physical and cognitive conditions”

This expression avoids both the abstract “everything” and paternalism: the goal is not to overwhelm the elderly person with technical information, but to adapt content, language, timing, and communication channels based on their sensory, cognitive, and emotional capacities. Best practices recommend: using clear, non-technical language; breaking information down into sequential steps; verifying understanding; respecting any limits or refusals to be informed about certain aspects; and, if necessary, involving support figures (family members, a guardian) without removing the older adult from the decision-making process.

Role of family members and “those who interact”

Assigning a responsibility to family members as well as to professionals means recognizing that many important decisions (regarding health, housing, and financial and care matters) are made within the domestic and relational context, not just in the doctor’s office. However, health and bioethical regulations emphasize that family members

Physical and geographic access: In many low- and middle-income countries, older adults live in rural or remote areas, far from hospitals, care centers, or public service offices, with inadequate transportation infrastructure and few local services. Access becomes even more challenging in the absence of integrated services, transportation, caregivers, or family support networks;

Socioeconomic inequalities—such as poverty, lack of health insurance, low levels of education, and discrimination—exacerbate difficulties in accessing information and services, particularly among older women, ethnic minorities, and populations in underserved areas, inevitably limiting their options and true freedom of choice.

The challenges in obtaining accurate information inevitably affect caregivers as well, who in turn need to be trained and informed. Only 16% of low-income countries offer training programs for informal caregivers; fewer than 60% include long-term care in their national programs.

Fulvio is 79 years old; he worked as an engineer, designing elevators. He worked in Switzerland and the Netherlands. He later became a manager at a company in La Spezia, and when the company secured contracts in Rome, he gladly moved to the capital. His pension allows him to live comfortably, but when his first health problems arose, his grandchildren advised him to move to a “very good” nursing home located outside Rome. Fulvio, initially very uncertain, allowed himself to be persuaded that, after an initial period of care, he would regain his strength and return home. Yes, because he has a beautiful home in the Piazza Sempione area waiting for him. At the same time, his grandchildren file a request for guardianship, believing it would be best for someone to assist him with financial management and daily decisions. He only learns of this initiative when he receives a summons from the Civil Court of Rome. His grandchildren downplay the matter and insist that it will be a significant help to him. They are convinced that, knowing their uncle’s eccentricities, an outsider is better suited as a guardian than they are—since their elderly uncle has never listened to them. Thus, a lawyer is appointed who suddenly intrudes into his private life, even into its most remote corners.

Well, thinks Fulvio, now I want to assert my rights: I’ll explain that first and foremost I want to go home, and maybe I’ll pay for a home care assistant to help me.

He prepares a nice speech, but at the first meeting he doesn’t sense much willingness to listen on the part of the lawyer, who, after showing the appointment decree, is in a hurry to have the ATM card, documents, and house keys handed over to him. Fulvio tells himself that maybe it wasn’t the right day—after all, it’s only the first meeting—and continues to think that if the judge decided this way, it means this is the path to asserting his rights and his requests. But after the first meeting, he no longer gets a chance to speak with the guardianship administration again. He asks the nursing home management to call him, but they tell him not to worry: “he’ll get in touch.” Fulvio protests, and they tell him to watch what he says, because they’ll report everything to the lawyer. So he tells everything to his friends who visit him from time to time. Somehow, they manage to speak with the guardian, and in response, he warns them not to keep meddling in Fulvio’s affairs and creating false hopes for him. He adds that he doesn’t want to take on the responsibility of bringing Fulvio home. This is the best situation—obviously best for him. End of discussion. Fulvio’s friends point out to him that he owns a beautiful house where, thanks in part to his

income, he could live comfortably. The guardian refuses to listen to reason and insists that things are fine as he has already decided. They insist that Fulvio’s wishes are different. The lawyer flies into a rage: “What wishes and wishes—we have to be realistic! And besides, I don’t have to explain to you why I made this decision. I have nothing further to add.”

Fulvio talks to everyone only about his home and being able to go out, but he can no longer speak with his guardian and never sees him.

He can’t understand how it’s possible that a stranger, someone he’s never seen before, can decide everything for him without listening to his wishes.

An older person has the right to receive adequate support in making their own decisions, including through the appointment of a trusted individual who, at their request and in accordance with their wishes and preferences, assists them in their decision-making.

In old age, as we have already seen, it is easy to find oneself in a shadow, seemingly due to one’s health and frailty. On closer inspection, it is much more often a matter of a pre-

prejudice based on ageism, a subtle desire to strip older people of their decision-making capacity and autonomy.

It is necessary to distinguish between an assessment of physical or cognitive dependence and the presumed inability to make decisions, which is often transformed into an implicit prohibition.

Mario is 82 years old and has some physical limitations. To get around, he needs the support of a walker and a little help getting to the bathroom. He has a decent pension after 40 years of work, and he has also been granted a caregiver’s allowance. He lives in public housing that was assigned to him when he was still young and his son was only 15. A few years ago, his son moved in with him after being evicted from the home where he lived with his family.

One day, out of the blue, his son tells him that living together is no longer possible: both he and his wife have to go to work and cannot take care of him during the day. He suggests a nursing home, but Mario tries to resist. His son’s proposal—which is now more than just a suggestion—upsets him, and to assert his rights, he fights back with all his might, sometimes even letting his anger resurface...

quarrelsome nature. Mario adopts these attitudes because he knows that, in reality, he will not be able to convince his son: the decision has already been made. He cries, he despairs, but he is forced to do what his son demands: he takes a bag with a few clothes, a phone, his glasses, and, together with his son, he sets off, without speaking, toward an isolated villa bordering the countryside and facing a busy road. Upon his arrival, an assistant greets him and shows him the room he is supposed to share with two other people. Some elderly residents look at him; a few greet him.

So, in the public housing unit registered under Mario’s name, his son remains to live with his family, and Mario—no longer considered part of the family—is forced to live in a facility among strangers, isolated from everyone and everything.

All he has left is his cell phone to maintain some contact. So he calls someone he knows and tells his absurd story, which feels like a nightmare from which he can no longer wake up. He says he feels miserable there, uncomfortable, that the food isn’t good—in fact, there isn’t enough of it, and he’s always hungry. A few days later, his son, having learned of his phone calls, goes to the facility and takes the phone away from him. He tells the director that it’s better not to let him keep it: those calls upset him and make him feel bad.

Mario could no longer tell anyone about these things; they had silenced him.

title_en: Charter, Art. 2 — The Right to Dignity (part 1)
text:
Charter, Art. 2 — The Right to Dignity

An older person has the right to preserve their dignity even in cases of partial or total loss of autonomy.

Many documents dedicated to the elderly emphasize that the loss of certain abilities (washing oneself, managing money, moving around) cannot automatically be equated with a judgment of “incapacity” or a sort of de facto incapacitation. Functional autonomy and moral autonomy are not the same: a person may be dependent in terms of hygiene or mobility and yet remain fully capable of desiring, choosing, and expressing preferences and values.

In this context, preserving dignity means:

being treated as people, not as “cases” or

“beds,” being called by name, with respect and without infantilization or sarcasm;

having one’s modesty, privacy, and physical and mental integrity protected during care and assistance, avoiding harmful practices such as restraints, forced feeding, or neglect.

Dignity also implies the right to participate in social and cultural life and to lead, as far as possible, a dignified and independent life, as affirmed by Article 25 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union.

Implications for families, services, and institutions

If dignity remains intact even in the face of lack of self-sufficiency, it becomes unacceptable to justify humiliations, exclusions, or violence “because the person doesn’t understand anyway” or “is no longer autonomous.” This gives rise to specific duties for caregivers: to personalize care, respect preferences, support remaining abilities, ensure access to care, income support, mobility, and social interaction, organizing services in a way that promotes (rather than restricts) autonomy and inclusion.

In summary, the article affirms a strong principle: the loss of autonomy may require more help and protection, but it never justifies the loss of dignity, which remains the ultimate criterion for judging the ethical, legal, and organizational quality of all practices directed toward older adults.

Older adults have the right to be called by name and treated with respect and tenderness.

The growing aging of the population, the evolution of the epidemiological landscape, and advances in medical science make it increasingly urgent to ensure that older adults have adequate access to palliative care and renewed human, social, and spiritual support. As highlighted in the relevant international literature, alongside the general principles on which palliative care is based (early identification, multidimensional assessment and care, continuity of care, and individualized planning of care and support pathways), it is necessary to consider the specific needs expressed by older patients and the ways in which these needs manifest themselves.

Adalgisa had worked in cabarets since she was 20. She loved to sing and dance and boasted to everyone that she had even met actors who later became famous. Everyone complimented her because she had a beautiful voice and a magnificent figure, as she herself said:

“Not for nothing, but I turned everyone’s heads.”

She was very particular about her clothing and always said that, once the war was over, she had finally been able to start buying new clothes and follow the fashion of the time.

She always recounts the same scenes while sitting, wrapped in her sheets, in the orthopedic bed of the four-bed room at the nursing home where she has been admitted for two years because “she could no longer be alone.” “What, can’t you walk? Why don’t you get up?” Adalgisa gestures to lower her voice and asks her listener to come a little closer. “Let’s speak quietly; even the walls have ears here. You see, I’ve always dressed a certain way—don’t imagine anything fancy, but never a hair out of place, never a stain on my clothes… here they make me wear a tracksuit because they say it’s more comfortable. But for whom is it more comfortable? For them. As for the tracksuit—and I suspect this one I’m wearing isn’t even mine—I was saying, I’ve never worn a tracksuit in my life; I’ve never liked them, and I’ve never even done gymnastics—dancing was enough exercise for me. Here, though, everyone wears tracksuits, men and women alike; sometimes they cut your hair so short you can barely tell a person’s gender. In tracksuits, we’re all the same. I obviously didn’t serve in the military, but it’s worse than a barracks here. I never get any visitors, but it’s better that way because I’d be ashamed to let anyone see me in this state. I’d really love to have an elegant dress and go out for a walk in the city.” How much does it cost the state, society, to dress an elderly woman properly?

Anyone who interacts with older adults has a duty to behave in a considerate, respectful, thoughtful, and courteous manner, and to listen and pay adequate attention to the concerns and observations raised by older adults .

A widespread habit, especially in care facilities, is addressing older adults in an impersonal and disrespectful manner. Calling an older adult by falsely familiar terms or replacing their name with an identification number are two seemingly opposite ways of relating, but both denote a lack of respect for the older adult.

This lack of respect often manifests itself in a lack of attention to the elderly person’s physical appearance: swapping clothing among residents and the use of poor-quality, impersonal clothing fall under this category of abuse.

The elderly person has the right to privacy, dignity, and respect for modesty in acts of personal and bodily care.

text:
Charter, Art. 2 — The Right to Dignity

This article emphasizes the need to view the elderly person not merely as a recipient of health or care services, but as a bearer of inviolable rights that extend even into the most vulnerable moments of life, such as those related to personal hygiene, bodily care, or medical procedures.

The three rights of the person

Right to privacy: this entails the protection of the elderly person’s private sphere, both in the handling of personal and health data and in the protection of physical spaces during care. No care-related act should take place in contexts that violate their privacy.

Right to dignity: this means ensuring that every intervention is carried out in a respectful and non-humiliating manner, recognizing the person’s intrinsic dignity even when they are dependent on the help of others. Dignity concerns the way in which the elderly person is spoken to, looked at, touched, and accompanied.

Respect for modesty: this emphasizes sensitivity toward the person’s perception of their own body and privacy, which varies according to culture, gender, and personal history. Care staff must adapt to these sensitivities and create an environment of trust and discretion.

2.J. The elderly person has the right to be supported in their remaining abilities even in the most compromised and terminal situations.

This article expresses a highly valuable ethical and care principle that places the continuity of the person’s dignity and autonomy at the center until the very last moment of life.

“To be supported in one’s remaining capacities” means recognizing that, even when physical, cognitive, or relational conditions are severely compromised, the person always retains some potential, however minimal—a gesture, a glance, a preference, an emotional response. These capacities must be supported, valued, and not replaced, because they represent the essence of subjectivity and personal identity.

The phrase “even in the most compromised and terminal situations” highlights the centrality of palliative care and nurturing, which is distinct from mere “treatment.” In such situations, the task of the care system is not only to alleviate physical pain but also to preserve quality of life, emotional communication, and relational presence. Title V of the Charter will return to these topics.

Ethical and Professional Implications

This principle is rooted in the idea that every person possesses intrinsic value regardless of their functional abilities. Care must therefore be oriented not only toward survival, but toward the promotion of human dignity, understood as respect for freedom, identity, and meaningful relationships.

In practice, this implies:

encouraging the older adult’s active participation in decision-making, as much as possible;

adapting care interventions to the remaining functional capacity;

promoting an empathetic relational environment free from frequent infantilizing approaches;

In summary, the phrase recalls one of the cornerstones of the ethics of care: never abandon the person in their fragility, but help them live fully until the end, maintaining self-awareness and respect for their own rhythms and desires.

title: Charter, Art. 3 — The Right to Psychophysical Integrity (part 1)
title_en: Charter, Art. 3 — The Right to Psychophysical Integrity (part 1)
text:
Charter, Art. 3 — The Right to Psychophysical Integrity

The elderly person has the right to the protection of their psychological and physical integrity and to be safeguarded from all forms of physical and moral violence and from improper forms of physical, pharmacological, and environmental restraint, as well as from abuse and intentional or unintentional neglect.

In order to decisively combat all forms of violence against older adults, consideration could be given to introducing aggravating circumstances in cases of moral and physical violence, mistreatment, deprivation of basic care, threats, extortion, humiliation, intimidation, and economic or financial violence, especially when such acts occur in protected settings or in care or assistance facilities. Particularly important is the fight against all forms of inappropriate physical, pharmacological, and environmental restraint. Such protection should be ensured regardless of whether the violence,

abuse, or neglect occurs at home, within an institution, or elsewhere.

The most effective form of prevention against this type of abuse is not the use of mere technological surveillance, such as video cameras, but the opportunity for older adults to cultivate social relationships and interact with the outside world even within care settings: the presence of visitors and volunteers constitutes the best protection against abuse that may occur in closed spaces.

A further preventive measure is the right of older adults to choose where and with whom they live, including through the promotion of home care services and co-housing as options accessible to all.

Guaranteeing this right requires public protection by institutions and administrations, which are called upon to find suitable solutions to prevent processes of marginalization. To this end, institutions must provide appropriate aids, not only those intended for the visually impaired, the hearing impaired, or for mobility, but also for social and digital participation.

Furthermore, the concrete and verifiable possibility of access to day centers represents an indispensable form of protection for these rights.

The right of older adults to engage in the activities of their choice must not be overlooked, including

work and apprenticeships, albeit through appropriate, effectively feasible, and available forms. A widespread prejudice leads people to believe that older adults are incapable of activity and engagement. Scientific evidence shows that active aging in old age, which not only ensures longer survival but also a slower decline, results in a lower demand for social and health services and a better quality of life.

Anyone who interacts with older adults has a duty to report any form of abuse, violence, or discrimination against them.

Giovanni is nearly 90 years old and has a very sharp mind. One thing, in particular, is clear to him: he does not want to go to a nursing home. He repeats this to everyone, partly to keep reminding himself. Of course, the future worries him. He is in good health but has no relatives, only a kind neighbor who does his grocery shopping and other errands. And whom he has always rewarded. His home is very well organized, but it’s on the third floor

without an elevator, it has become difficult for him to go out. One day, a small pothole in the courtyard proves fatal. He falls: a fractured femur.

Thus begins a journey he had always feared. The neighbor who visits him confides her concerns about his return home: she cannot help him any more than she has so far. She also spoke with the doctors and the hospital social worker, explaining that she could do very little, and then there was also the issue of managing his pension, household expenses, and everything else… In short, he had no one. For this reason, the social services decided to immediately file a request for a guardian. It’s not that Giovanni wasn’t capable of deciding how to manage his money and his future, but he is a 90-year-old man, and in the absence of a relative, the simplest solution seems to be to entrust him to an institutional figure.

Meanwhile, once the acute phase is over, they also decide to transfer him to another facility. Not exactly rehabilitation, since he is an elderly man, but post-acute rehabilitation: a lower intensity of rehabilitative care. So he does only a few minutes of rehabilitation a day and then spends the rest of the time in bed: no one gets him up. It’s easy to imagine how little this rehabilitation helps him significantly recover his motor skills.

One day, a doctor from the facility approaches his bed and explains that it would be better for him to continue his treatment by transferring to another facility

just outside Rome, but a very good one, near Velletri. For the transfer, he would have to sign the form the doctor was insistently handing him: “Here, you have to sign here.” Giovanni hesitates; he doesn’t understand. He’d like to talk about his future to prepare for his return home; he’d like explanations about his health condition; he’d like to ask why he still can’t walk… and so many other things: in short, he’d like to talk to someone. But his time is up; the doctor is in a hurry and has already started addressing another patient. He manages only to say: “But I’d like to go home.” The doctor looks at him with pity, as if he were rambling:

“Of course, but now you have to stay here.” Giovanni finally signs, without knowing what it’s for. Without realizing it, he has just given his consent for a transfer to a nursing home. After that signature, the months pass without anyone explaining anything to him anymore. He waits to continue his rehabilitation, but every day, for some reason, it gets postponed.

One day, a stranger appears at his bedside: “Good morning, I’m Attorney Bianchi. I’ve been appointed as your guardian. I’ll handle your pension and whatever else you need.” Giovanni begins to see a way out. “Well, I’d like to go home; I’ve been here for five months already.” The lawyer replies without leaving room for argument: “It’s still too early to leave; we’ll talk about it later. In the meantime, I’ll handle the payment

the fees for this facility. Then we’ll see. I’ll come back to visit you when I can, because this place is far from Rome.” Giovanni asks for access to some money because he has nothing with him and might need something. The lawyer’s response is even more blunt: “What do you need money for here? You’re not missing anything; they take care of everything.”

Giovanni is still waiting for someone to explain to him why he has to stay in there.

The elderly person has the right to maintain and have their beliefs, opinions, and feelings respected.

Empirical literature and policies on healthy/active aging consistently show that respect for the elderly person’s beliefs, values, and emotional experiences—that is, a truly person-centered approach—is associated with better psychological well-being, a higher quality of life, and reduced reliance on avoidable healthcare services and hospitalizations. European and international charters of rights and guidelines on the care of older adults translate this evidence into operational recommendations, calling on services to recognize and honor life histories, beliefs

and preferences, even when they diverge from the dominant culture.

Qualitative studies in nursing homes describe older adults who find the imposition of rigid routines (meal times, hygiene, activities) without any choice to be humiliating, feeling that they “must obey” and cannot express opinions or desires regarding daily aspects relevant to their dignity. Some residents report feeling dehumanized, with a “restricted” identity, because they cannot express their tastes, clothing style, religious preferences, or social preferences as they did at home. A brief review of human rights in nursing homes highlights cases where older adults complain that their preferences (for example, regarding who assists them with hygiene, whether or not to participate in religious services, or the management of personal belongings) are systematically ignored in the name of institutional efficiency. These situations are described as genuine threats to dignity, accompanied by feelings of coercion and a loss of inner freedom.

J

text:
Charter, Art. 4 — The duty to combat abuse and ageism

Society has a duty to prevent and ensure that no abuse is perpetrated against individuals in care settings, whether residential, community-based, or home-based.

Society as a whole has a duty to build a multi-level protection system that makes abuse against older adults difficult to commit, easy to detect, and subject to punishment, in any care setting (nursing homes, community facilities, or at home). But how can one protect oneself from abuse?

Regulatory and Institutional Level

The state must establish effective criminal and civil laws against mistreatment, neglect, and abusive or inadequate facilities, holding accountable even those who fail to prevent abuse (omission of supervision).

Health and judicial authorities must organize periodic and targeted inspections of facilities,

with the authority to suspend operations and transfer residents in cases of serious violations, as demonstrated by NAS inspections and the closure of non-compliant facilities.

Regulatory Framework and Guidelines

Regions and local authorities have a duty to define structural, organizational, and staffing requirements for nursing homes, residential communities, group homes, and home care services, linking authorization and accreditation to compliance with safety and quality standards.

Guidelines and protocols must be established for the prevention, identification, and management of abuse (such as the “Zero Abuse” project, a training, research, and intervention initiative promoted by UPIPA (Provincial Union of Care Institutions, Trentino) between 2017 and 2019, developed in collaboration with Prof. Luca Fazzi), with clear procedures for observation, internal reporting, resident protection, and notification to the competent authority.

Organizational and Professional Level

Organizations providing care have a duty to train staff in recognizing abuse (physical, psychological, financial, and neglect), conflict management, and a culture of rights, avoiding the “normalization” of abusive practices.

Secure reporting channels must be provided

(including anonymous reporting) for staff, family members, and residents, audit procedures for adverse events, and zero-tolerance policies toward harmful behavior, as indicated by recent guidelines and protocols.

Community and cultural level

Civil society (associations, unions, professional associations, media) has a duty to bring to light the “silent violence” against older adults, breaking the invisibility of the phenomenon and promoting public awareness.

The community must combat ageism, support caregivers, and promote neighborhood and volunteer networks that reduce isolation, a crucial risk factor for abuse, including in the home.

Data on abuse and mistreatment

Abuse and mistreatment (a “hard” indicator of prejudice)

Globally, a 2025 review estimates that approximately 27.6% of older adults experience some form of abuse, with psychological abuse and neglect being the most prevalent.

Charter, Art. 4 — The duty to combat abuse and ageism

In Europe, the WHO report cites approximately 4 million older adults as victims of physical and psychological abuse each year, with over 10 million experiencing long-term consequences.

In Italy, recent studies place the prevalence at

between 10% and 20%; a research estimate indicates that approximately 12.7% of older adults were victims of abuse in the past year, of which 10.4% was psychological and 2.6–2.7% financial.

In nursing homes and residential facilities

SIGG has estimated that approximately 1 in 3 older adults in nursing homes has experienced some form of abuse or neglect. These figures do not merely reflect “poor organization,” but also an underlying atmosphere of devaluation and dehumanization that is the typical breeding ground for prejudice.

Ageism and discrimination in care

One in two people worldwide reports age-based prejudice (ageism), which influences how they think and make decisions regarding older adults. In the healthcare context, ageism leads to approximately 4 in 10 older adults being excluded from the best and most appropriate care solely due to their chronological age, with an impact on survival and quality of life. A review of ageism among healthcare professionals highlights a general trend of “low self-reported rates,” but with significant variations: less geriatric training and higher work-related stress are associated with higher ageism scores.

In the context of dementia or cognitive frailty, studies on stigma and perceptions show that a significant proportion of caregivers view people with dementia as “impulsive and unpredictable,” with a risk of defensive or restrictive approaches.

Restraints

In many countries, the use of physical or pharmacological restraints on the elderly is still widespread, despite being recognized as a practice carrying high ethical and clinical risks; society’s duty is therefore to limit it to extremely rare, monitored, and transparent exceptions, rather than as a hidden routine.

The scope of the phenomenon worldwide

An international review of residential facilities indicates an “average” prevalence of physical restraint of around 26–33% of residents, with wide variation across countries and facilities.

In Europe, a multicenter study reported rates of physical restraint in elderly care facilities ranging from 7.7% to 60.5%; another survey cites average rates of 37% in Europe, 22% in North America, 31% in Canada, and 20% in Hong Kong.

In Asia, the percentages may be even higher: in 10 facilities in Hong Kong, a prevalence of physical restraint of 70.2% was reported, while in a recent study in South Korea, 79.5% of nursing homes used forms of restraint, and in over 20% of cases for more than 8 hours a day.

In the hospital setting

Among older adults admitted to acute care wards, some reviews report rates of physical restraint ranging from 33% to 68%.

In rehabilitation settings, specific studies describe prevalence rates of around 12–13% of patients.

title: Charter, Art. 4 — The duty to combat abuse and ageism (part 3)
title_en: Charter, Art. 4 — The duty to combat abuse and ageism (part 3)
text:
Charter, Art. 4 — The duty to combat abuse and ageism

Society has a duty to prevent and counteract the various forms of physical or pharmacological restraint, ensuring adequate oversight of these facilities by the various public social and health agencies, and where present, by authorities responsible for defending and guaranteeing the rights of the elderly.

Focus on pharmacological restraint worldwide

“Chemical” restraint (the use of medications not for a primary clinical indication, but to restrain or sedate) is equally significant: a meta-analysis of residential facilities reports an average prevalence of pharmacological restraint (psychotropic drugs/antipsychotics as “behavioral control”) of around 32%.

In the United States, prior to reduction campaigns, approximately 1 in 3 residents with dementia in nursing homes was taking antipsychotics, often in a potentially inappropriate manner; following the “National Partnership to Improve Dementia Care,” the potential use

inappropriate use has decreased by 33%, but remains a significant problem.

In Canada, in 2025, approximately 1 in 4 long-term care residents is taking a potentially unnecessary antipsychotic, according to data from Choosing Wisely Canada. These figures show that pharmacological restraint is a widespread phenomenon, often less visible than physical restraint but no less harmful to rights and health.

How should we respond to the phenomenon of restraint?

Ethical Implications: A “Systemic Failure”

The literature is unanimous in emphasizing that physical restraint is neither safe nor effective in preventing falls or accidents, and is instead associated with increased physical risks (injuries, pressure sores, suffocation) and psychological risks (fear, loss of trust, experience of punishment). The inappropriate use of antipsychotics in older adults with dementia is also linked to increased mortality, cardiovascular events, and infections, to the extent that it has prompted the issuance of regulatory black box warnings.

In this context, the widespread use of physical restraints often indicates:

organizational shortcomings (staff shortages, insufficient training, unsafe environments);

defensive professional cultures, which view the elderly person as a “problem to be contained” rather than as an individual to be understood and supported.

Duties of Society and the Authorities

In light of these findings, the statement that “society has a duty to prevent and combat various forms of restraint” implies:

the existence of regulations and standards: national and regional policies that explicitly discourage the use of restraint, define restrictive criteria (last resort, documented clinical justification, limited duration), and require mandatory recording of every instance of physical or chemical restraint;

title: Charter, Art. 4 — The duty to combat abuse and ageism (part 4)
title_en: Charter, Art. 4 — The duty to combat abuse and ageism (part 4)
text:
Charter, Art. 4 — The duty to combat abuse and ageism

oversight and inspections: monitoring systems for facilities (residential, community-based, and hospital-based) with specific indicators on physical restraint and the use of psychotropic drugs, targeted inspections, and the possibility of sanctions, suspension, or revocation of authorizations and accreditations.

Examples of ageism around the world

A testimony reported by Amnesty International tells the story of Akua Denteh,* a 90-year-old woman, who was lynched to death in 2020 after being publicly accused of witchcraft; the lynching was even filmed and shared online, sparking national outrage.

* Amnesty International, “Branded for Life: How Witchcraft Accusations Lead to Human Rights Violations of Hundreds of Women in North Ghana.” www.amnesty.org/en/documents/afr28/9099/2025/en./

Women in the camps, many of whom are between 50 and 90 years old, are subjected to summary trials, purification rituals, and the deprivation of their human rights: they live in mud huts, isolated from the rest of society, without access to adequate food, medical care, or protection. These cases are rarely reported or investigated. Accusations of witchcraft can lead to threats, physical assault, or even death. They usually arise within family contexts or among community members following a tragic event such as an illness or a death. Older women living in poverty, with health problems or disabilities, are at greater risk, as are women who do not conform to gender stereotypes.

In Tanzania, a report by the Legal and Human Rights Centre cites over 2,500 elderly women killed between 2004 and 2009 on suspicion of witchcraft in rural regions. Widows are often accused for inheritance-related reasons: superstition serves as a pretext to deprive women of their assets or to expel them from the community.

“My neighbor said he dreamed […] that I was trying to kill him. He doesn’t want me [in the community], that’s why he accused me,” said Fawza,a resident of the Gnani camp. “I refused to let the [village] chief marry one of my daughters. One day, a little girl fell ill in the community and the chief accused me,” said Fatma, a resident of the Kukuo camp.

Society has a duty to prevent and counteract all forms of ageism and to develop appropriate responses to specific forms of ageism, depending on their cultural and geographical distribution, since prejudice and marginalization take different forms in different geographical, ethnic, and cultural contexts.

According to WHO data, approximately 1 in 6 older adults (141 million people) experienced some form of abuse in the community over the past year.

If the proportion of older adults who are victims of abuse remains constant, the number of people affected in their communities will rise rapidly due to population aging, increasing to 320 million victims by 2050.

About 1 in 6 people over the age of 60 has experienced some form of abuse in their community over the past year.

title: Charter, Art. 4 — The duty to combat abuse and ageism (part 5)
title_en: Charter, Art. 4 — The duty to combat abuse and ageism (part 5)
text:
Charter, Art. 4 — The duty to combat abuse and ageism

Rates of elder abuse are high in institutions such as nursing homes and long-term care facilities, with 2 in 3 reporting that abuse occurred last year.

Elder abuse can lead to serious physical injuries and long-term psychological consequences.

Elder abuse is expected to increase as many countries are experiencing rapid population aging.

The global population of people aged 60 and older will more than double, from 900 million in 2015 to approximately 2 billion in 2050.

According to the WHO, elder abuse is a single or repeated act, or a failure to act, occurring within any relationship where there is an expectation of trust, that causes harm or distress to an older person.

This type of violence constitutes a violation of human rights and includes physical, sexual, psychological, and emotional abuse; financial and material abuse; neglect; and severe loss of dignity and respect. For the WHO, elder abuse is a major public health issue. A 2017 study based on the best available evidence from 52 studies in 28 countries across different regions, including 12 low- and middle-income countries, estimated that, in the past year, 15.7% of people aged 60 and older had experienced some form of abuse. This is likely an underestimate, as only 1 in 24 cases of elder abuse is reported, partly because older adults are often afraid to report abuse to family members, friends, or

the authorities.

Consequently, prevalence rates are likely to be underestimated. Although the

rigorous data are limited, the study provides prevalence estimates, based on all available studies, of the number of older adults affected by different types of abuse.

Data on the extent of the problem in institutions such as hospitals, nursing homes, and other long-term care facilities are scarce. However, systematic reviews and meta-analyses of recent studies on elder abuse in these institutional and community settings, based on self-reports by older adults, suggest that abuse rates are much higher in institutions than in community settings.

Schools must implement intergenerational education by fostering and strengthening young people’s relationships with older adults.łł Forms of civic engagement promoting solidarity with older adults and combating ageism must be promoted in every country.ł7

The fight against ageism also involves formal and informal educational programs that highlight the contribution of older adults to the social, cultural, and economic life of communities. In line with these principles, Law No. of March 23, 2023, provides for the promotion of experiences of solidarity and

intergenerational cultural initiatives, aimed at fostering the transmission of cultural heritage and strengthening cohesion between generations.

title: Charter, Art. 4 — The duty to combat abuse and ageism (part 6)
title_en: Charter, Art. 4 — The duty to combat abuse and ageism (part 6)
text:
Charter, Art. 4 — The duty to combat abuse and ageism

Legislative Decree No. of March 15, 2024, No. 29, implementing Law 33/2023, identifies schools as a privileged setting for encounters and dialogue between young people and older adults and promotes educational projects and activities at all levels of the education system, including initiatives for active citizenship and the reduction of the digital divide through the direct involvement of students in support of older adults.

At the international level, UN and European Union documents explicitly refer to intergenerational solidarity as a component of social sustainability, calling on countries to promote policies and programs that connect young people and older adults, not only on an emotional level, but as a social and political responsibility of every community. Active citizenship initiatives involve young people engaged in social projects for older adults (home visits, digital support, co-design of community services), often supported by programs from United Nations agencies and sustainable development organizations.

Best practices in schools

Intergenerational school programs: in various countries (the U.S., Canada, the U.K.), elementary and secondary schools regularly involve

in educational activities, reading, oral history workshops, mentoring, and community service projects.

School-based intergenerational programs involve schools utilizing older adults’ resources to support students’ learning (e.g., homework help, craft workshops, historical memory) and, in return, young people contributing to the practical needs of older adults (digital literacy, assistance with services, recreational activities).

International guidelines on best practices highlight recurring elements: activities prepared collaboratively (teachers-staff-seniors), voluntary participation, post-activity reflection in the classroom, age- and role-appropriate activities, and a focus on collaboration and mutual exchange.

Explicit education against ageism

Educational programs on stereotypes and discrimination: in various Anglo-Saxon contexts, learning units are offered on what ageism is, how prejudices toward older adults manifest, and how to recognize one’s own distorted perceptions.

Educational projects co-designed with older adults: recent studies demonstrate the effectiveness of platforms and workshops developed in collaboration with older adults to raise young people’s awareness of ageism, combining theoretical education with meaningful intergenerational engagement.

Key elements of good practice

Centrality of meaningful, not just occasional, contact: repeated meetings with shared goals and clear roles for young people and older adults.

Mutual benefit: the most effective programs are those in which both generations learn, teach, and produce something together (projects, services, testimonials).

Curricular integration: intergenerational education works best when it is part of the curriculum (civics, history, social sciences), not just an extracurricular activity.

title: Charter, Art. 4 — The duty to combat abuse and ageism (part 7)
title_en: Charter, Art. 4 — The duty to combat abuse and ageism (part 7)
text:
Charter, Art. 4 — The duty to combat abuse and ageism

4.J. Society has a duty to promote among older adults themselves the fight against ageist stereotypes that so often influence them and contribute to forms of self-marginalization. Promoting a positive image of old age as a season of life with its own positive potential is in the collective interest.

The article offers a very interesting shift: it moves the focus from merely protecting the elderly to their active role in combating stereotypes, while simultaneously highlighting the collective interest in a positive portrayal of old age.

Involvement of the elderly

The reference to “combating ageist stereotypes among the elderly themselves” highlights a crucial phenomenon: the internalization of prejudice, that is, the adoption by the elderly of negative self-images that fuel resignation, passivity, and self-marginalization.

The article states that it is up to society to create the conditions—including cultural, educational, and communicative contexts—that enable older adults to recognize these stereotypes, distance themselves from them, and value their own resources, thereby fostering social participation, civic engagement, and the continuity of their life plans.

Originality and Uniqueness of the Principle

Compared to many charters of the rights of older adults, which focus on protection, assistance, and combating “suffered” abuse and discrimination, this article introduces an original element: the idea of anti-ageist empowerment of older adults themselves, not merely external protection.

Particularly significant is the link between a positive image of old age and the “interest of the community itself”: it moves beyond a purely welfare-oriented view to assert that active aging—recognized and socially valued—constitutes social, cultural, and economic capital for society as a whole (transfer of skills, informal care, volunteering, historical memory, intergenerational cohesion).

Cultural and Political Value

The article introduces a strong cultural perspective: it is not enough to defend the elderly from the ageism “of others”; it is necessary to transform social representations of old age and, at the same time, support the elderly in freeing themselves from the self-stereotypes that block desires, initiative, and participation.

In this sense, the text is truly unique: it entrusts older adults with the task of building a movement of genuine revolt—first and foremost internal and personal—against ageist prejudices, thereby laying the political foundations for a new vision of old age.

title: Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection (part 1)
title_en: Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection (part 1)
text:
Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection

Older persons have the right to their own livelihood, in particular to secure access to food, water, shelter, adequate clothing, and care.

Here, a distinction must be made between two radically different scenarios: that of developed countries and, in contrast, the challenges faced by countries with limited resources.

DEVELOPED COUNTRIES

In two-thirds of OECD countries, poverty is more common among older adults than in the general population. Older adults living alone, especially women, more often experience housing hardship—that is, difficulty covering high housing costs, managing unexpected expenses, handling maintenance work, dealing with bureaucracy, and negotiating with landlords. To make matters worse, ethnic minorities, older migrants, and people with disabilities face

face greater barriers in accessing decent and safe neighborhoods, compounded by historical disadvantages such as redlining and gentrification.

Redlining

This is a practice that originated in the United States in the 20th century: banks, insurance companies, and institutions literally drew red lines on maps to mark neighborhoods considered “high-risk” (often inhabited by racial minorities or poor groups) and systematically denied mortgages, loans, insurance policies, or investments in those areas. In essence, this means excluding entire urban areas from access to credit and services based not on individual criteria, but on collective ones (neighborhood, race, social composition).

The result is a vicious cycle: building deterioration, concentrated poverty, fewer educational and employment opportunities, and de facto segregation, even without formal segregation laws.

Redlining can also affect older adults: in urban areas marked by disinvestment (suburban or deteriorated neighborhoods), where many older adults live alone or on low incomes, banking and insurance policies can effectively result in exclusion from credit (mortgages, renovation loans, home insurance) because the area is “red” or considered high-risk from a socio-economic perspective. When advanced age is compounded by other factors (poverty, ethnicity, gender),

the effect of territorial redlining creates a double disadvantage: not only is the neighborhood penalized, but the elderly population within it is the least able to “move” or change their living situation.

Concrete examples of situations analogous to redlining

Access to credit and renovations: banks that, in neighborhoods with a high concentration of older adults and older homes, systematically deny small loans or mortgages for renovations, citing the applicant’s age and the “low value” of the area, thereby preventing safety upgrades, accessibility improvements, and energy-saving measures.

title: Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection (part 2)
title_en: Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection (part 2)
text:
Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection

Insurance and healthcare services: Insurance companies that charge exorbitant premiums or refuse to issue health or long-term care policies in areas with a high proportion of frail older adults—deemed “too risky”—effectively creating zones where access to insurance coverage is nearly impossible.

Infrastructure and public services: suburban neighborhoods with a high concentration of older adults where, due to political and planning decisions, public transportation, local social and health services, and community spaces are being reduced, while investments are concentrated in “young” and highly profitable areas. This results in a genuine “infrastructural exclusion” of entire older adult communities.

Real estate market and nursing homes: areas with a high concentration of low-income older adults where

real estate operators and residential facility managers do not invest, resulting in a supply of housing and services of lower quality compared to other neighborhoods that are more “attractive” demographically and economically.

In analytical terms, it can be said that older adults are often victims of intersectional redlining (age

+ location + income), which limits access to credit, services, infrastructure, and opportunities, contributing to the entrenchment of vulnerability and isolation.

Gentrification

Gentrification refers to the process by which a working-class neighborhood—often central or semi-central, with dilapidated buildings—is “redeveloped,” properties are renovated, prices and rents rise, and the original, less affluent population is gradually replaced by the middle and upper-middle classes.

This process has two sides: on the one hand, urban renewal, improved services, and increased perceived safety; on the other, the displacement of long-time residents, the loss of social and cultural networks, and rising costs of living and housing.

It is therefore a process that is both physical (change in the built environment) and social (change in

class composition of the neighborhood), typical of contemporary large cities and post-industrial economies.

The best response to these phenomena appears to be the promotion of initiatives for solidarity-based, senior, or intergenerational cohabitation, which also take on the role of urban redevelopment and regeneration, particularly in the peripheral, historic, or run-down neighborhoods of our cities.

Cohousing

Solidarity-based living arrangements and forms of intergenerational cohabitation represent a privileged tool for combating loneliness, redlining, and gentrification that is detrimental to the elderly, by promoting inclusion, mutual aid, and the social regeneration of urban contexts. This solution:10

correctly links shared living, the fight against loneliness, and social inclusion—which are explicitly mentioned, for example, among the objectives of Italian Law 33/2023;

title: Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection (part 3)
title_en: Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection (part 3)
text:
Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection

recognizes that new forms of community living (cohousing, supportive cohabitation) can constitute a “bottom-up” response to processes of exclusion: older adults who come together strengthen their bargaining power, access services, and maintain their roots in the community rather than being displaced or institutionalized.

Link to Law 33/2023

Law 33/2023, among its guiding principles and criteria, provides for:11

the “promotion of new forms of home-based living and solidarity-based cohabitation for older adults (senior cohousing) and intergenerational cohabitation, particularly with disadvantaged youth,” including through urban regeneration and the reuse of the built environment;

measures to combat social isolation and relational deprivation through listening initiatives, support for socialization, and the involvement of the third sector, volunteers, and civil service.

This means that the law not only “tolerates” supportive cohabitation, but adopts it as a tool of public policy, serving inclusion, active aging, and social cohesion.

COUNTRIES WITH LIMITED RESOURCES

In countries with limited resources, many older adults lack a stable pension income and depend on family or informal work. Consequently, there is a high prevalence of shantytowns, villages lacking basic services, and precarious housing exposed to climate risks and disasters,13 as well as a near-total absence of housing policies specifically designed for older adults. Property rights are poorly protected, with the risk of eviction or loss of housing following widowhood, migration, or conflict.

It is estimated that approximately 26 million older people are affected each year by disasters and humanitarian crises, many of which are linked to armed conflicts. By the end of 2023, approximately 10 million people aged 60 and older were living as refugees, accounting for about 8% of the 118 million forcibly displaced people worldwide; this number has nearly doubled since 2014. The proportion of older adults (aged 50+ or 60+) living in fragile countries at high risk of conflict and disasters will rise from approximately 12.3% (220 million people) in 2020 to over 19% (approximately 586 million) in 2050.

These figures refer only to those registered as refugees or displaced persons; many older adults remain in war zones and do not appear in the statistics, so the actual number of older adults affected by conflict is significantly higher.

Specific Risks for Older Adults in War

title: Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection (part 4)
title_en: Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection (part 4)
text:
Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection

Organizations such as Human Rights Watch, the UN, and HelpAge document that older adults are disproportionately affected by killings, violence, abandonment, loss of home, difficulty fleeing, and reduced access to food, healthcare, and assistance. Among forcibly displaced older adults, up to 14 million are people with disabilities, who are often completely excluded from humanitarian interventions. In summary, available data indicate that at least tens of millions of older adults are affected each year by conflicts and humanitarian crises, with this number increasing over time and likely being significantly underestimated due to the lack of statistical visibility of this population group.

Older adults have the right to the protection of their income and assets in order to maintain an adequate and dignified standard of living.

High-Income Countries: Data and Challenges

In OECD countries, on average 14.8% of people over 65 live in relative income poverty (below 50% of the median income), meaning that approximately one in seven older adults does not achieve an adequate standard of living even in wealthy contexts.

In 2024, the at-risk-of-poverty rate for older adults in the European Union is estimated to be around 16–17%, with higher rates among very elderly single women, indicating that the right to income security is most compromised among the very elderly and single-person households.

Some concrete examples of critical issues in resource-rich countries:

in South Korea, nearly 40% of people over 66 live in relative income poverty—the highest rate in the OECD—despite the country’s economic advancement; this is linked to pension systems that are still underdeveloped and fragmented work histories;23

in OECD countries where minimum pensions are low or weakly indexed (for example, some

Eastern European countries), there are statutory pensions that are

“inadequate,” which do not prevent a fall into poverty, forcing many older adults to continue working or to cut back on essential expenses (food, heating, healthcare).

The main issues that violate the stated right, even in wealthy contexts, are:

pensions insufficient to cover the cost of living, especially in the face of rising health and long-term care costs;25

erosion of assets (home, savings) to pay for long-term care or uncovered medications; in some cases, older adults end up selling their homes or depleting all their savings, losing housing security and independence;26

economic and financial abuse: the UN report highlights fraud, theft of assets, land expropriation, scams involving bank accounts and pensions, and the fraudulent use of legal capacity to control the elderly person’s assets and income.

Countries with limited resources: data and challenges

Globally, approximately 3. billion people have no social protection, and in low- and middle-income countries, many older adults reach old age without a pension, after a lifetime of informal work not covered by contributions.

title: Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection (part 5)
title_en: Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection (part 5)
text:
Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection

In low-income countries, on average one in three older adults experiences multidimensional poverty (deprivation of income, food, education, services, and housing), while in lower-middle-income countries the proportion is about “one in ten,” confirming that a decent standard of living is often out of reach in the absence of social safety nets. Global statistics show that, in developing countries, “almost all” working people over 65 are in informal jobs: the WIEGO report indicates that in developing countries, nearly all older workers are in informal jobs, and that among those aged 65 and older, the share of informal work is close to 100% of total employment.

In various contexts across Latin America and the Caribbean, national studies report that between 20% and over 35% of older adults (aged 60 or 65+) are still employed, with a male majority and a heavy reliance on self-employment and informal work.

UN and World Bank reports describe this “forced” participation as a response to the lack of pension income: those who have neither a pension nor savings cannot retire from work even under poor health conditions.

Some typical problems in resource-constrained contexts:

very low pension coverage: many older adults receive no pension and depend

entirely on family members, remittances, or work in old age; participation in pension programs remains stagnant precisely because of the prevalence of informal work;

absolute poverty: the proportion of older adults living below the extreme monetary poverty line is much higher than in wealthy countries; the ILO and the UN note that many older adults continue to work in old age out of sheer necessity, without protection or a stable income;34

property rights violations: the UN report on the human rights of older people describes cases of expropriation of land, homes, and assets, fraud, and the forcible removal of control over assets (imposed guardianship, extorted sales, and violence linked to traditional beliefs, such as the aforementioned accusations of witchcraft aimed at seizing assets).

Concrete examples of pension issues and informal work

Indonesia (middle-income country, high informality): A 2024 study reports that the percentage of older adults in the workforce is increasing and that “the majority” of employed older adults are in informal jobs; among working older adults, over 86% were in the informal sector in 2022. Working older women are even more exposed to

informality: in some years, over 90% of working older women are in informal occupations, often in micro-commerce, domestic services, and subsistence agriculture.

title: Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection (part 6)
title_en: Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection (part 6)
text:
Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection

India (a large middle-income economy with a strong informal sector): research cited in the same study indicates that approximately 73% of working older adults are engaged in informal activities, primarily agriculture, day labor, and small-scale services, with low and highly unstable incomes. The absence or meagerness of formal pensions drives older adults to remain active in physically demanding jobs, with documented negative consequences on health and cognitive function.

Dominican Republic: An analysis of older adults’ employment indicates that approximately 35% of older adults are still employed, with a clear prevalence of men (52% of older men work compared to 19% of women), and with estimated informality rates of around 85% among those over 60.

Older adults often work as street vendors, small-scale farmers, domestic workers, or in other uncontracted occupations; many already receive a minimal pension, but its amount does not allow for an adequate standard of living, so work necessarily supplements their income.

Older adults have the right, especially in the absence of a social security system, to employment opportunities commensurate with their experience, physical capacity, and health. They also have the right to access all other income-generating activities.

To make the right of older adults to adequate employment opportunities a reality, it is necessary to prevent all forms of age discrimination, thus banning age limits in job postings, monitoring discriminatory language in job offers (as in European initiatives such as “vacancies for all ages”), and abolishing automatic dismissal based on age, where it exists.

Above all, however, work must be adapted, tailored, and made flexible: part-time work, flexible hours, telecommuting, job-sharing, less physically demanding tasks, and “phased retirement” programs that reduce working hours while maintaining a decent income.

Other key areas of action include:

continuing education and specific retraining for older workers, with training vouchers, paid leave for courses, and mentoring in the use of technology;

“Age-friendly” public employment services: dedicated service counters, counseling for returning to work, and wage subsidies for employers who hire older adults in vulnerable situations.

Solutions in resource-constrained countries

Where social security is absent or minimal, the right enshrined in the article can be pursued through “low-cost but highly organized” policies:

support for self-employment and microenterprises run by older adults: microcredit programs, revolving funds, and training on small-scale activities (family farming, food processing, crafts, neighborhood commerce), with technical assistance;45

integration of older adults into rural and urban development programs: recognizing older adults as beneficiaries of land, tools, and small capital, rather than excluding them due to their age; including them in cooperative projects, producer associations, and local markets.
