title: Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection (part 7)
title_en: Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection (part 7)
text:
Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection

Access to credit without age discrimination is also crucial: many poor older adults cannot finance income-generating activities because they are considered “unbankable”; specific programs for older adults (including through NGOs, community savings groups, and religious associations) overcome this barrier.

HelpAge documents suggest complementing income-generating activities with initiatives addressing health, social isolation, and access to social transfers, as work should not replace a basic safety net.

Access to “other income-generating activities”

To give substance to the second paragraph, solutions include:

light cash-for-work programs: adapted community work (surveillance, educational support, cultural activities, maintenance of common spaces) with compensation that supplements income, tailored to the physical capabilities of older adults;

paid caregiving and mentoring roles: older adults engaged, with compensation, as child caregivers, community mediators, craft instructors, and custodians of local knowledge (e.g., traditional craft workshops), while ensuring this does not become a low-cost substitute for public services;

paid participation in cultural, tourism, or historical memory projects (local guides, storytellers, community archivists), which highlight the memory and expertise of the elderly;

mixed work-transfer schemes: combining small non-contributory pensions or social allowances with incentives to maintain, on a voluntary basis, micro-enterprise activities or light work, so that older adults are not forced to work but can choose.

In summary, policies that create opportunities for dignified work and income-generating activities for older adults, but always prioritizing their health and the freedom to choose whether and how much to work, rather than the need to compensate for the lack of social protection.

Older adults must be able to determine, in accordance with the legal framework in which they live, the timing and manner of their retirement from work, by accessing pension benefits that guarantee them a free and dignified existence.

The Right to Retire

This statement expresses a twofold right: the freedom to decide the timing and manner of retirement from work, and the entitlement to a pension adequate to guarantee a free and dignified existence. It is precisely in these two areas that serious imbalances and violations are emerging today.

The meaning of the stated right

The text follows in the footsteps of the UN Principles for Older Persons, which state that older people must be able to participate in determining “when and at what pace” to retire from work and live

“in dignity and security.”49

The reference to a pension that guarantees a free and dignified existence is consistent with the European Pillar of Social Rights, which recognizes the right to an adequate pension and to live with dignity in old age.

Issues regarding the “power to choose” retirement

source_label_en: Charter of the Rights of Older Persons
title: Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection (part 8)
title_en: Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection (part 8)
text:
Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection

In many legal systems, there are rigid retirement ages, mandatory placement requirements, or penalties

for those who choose to remain in the workforce or, conversely, for those forced to retire early due to health issues or caregiving responsibilities.

Studies on pension systems and the labor market show that the expectation to “work longer” ignores the fact that many older adults are unable to remain employed due to illness, age discrimination, or family caregiving responsibilities, with negative impacts on psychological well-being and social isolation.

Issues Regarding Pension Adequacy

European and international reports indicate that a significant proportion of pensions fall below relative or even absolute poverty thresholds, meaning they do not cover essential needs (housing, food, energy, healthcare). Research based on the direct experiences of older adults shows that many live on “too low” incomes, forced to cut back on healthcare, heating, or food, resulting in a loss of autonomy and the ability to make “choices” in daily life. In fact, the pension does not guarantee the dignified existence envisioned by the statement. Added to this is the elderly person’s inability to change course: retirement arrives at

a time when it is “too late” to change.

When freedom becomes constraint

The combination of inadequate pensions and labor markets hostile to the elderly creates a distortion:

those who would like to retire cannot do so because the pension

pension is insufficient and continue to work in precarious, often informal jobs;

those who would like to work longer by choice or because they have incomplete contribution histories face legal barriers (loss of benefits, limits on combining income) or age discrimination in the workplace. Finally, in many low- and middle-income countries, the

pension system means that old age entails total dependence on the family or forced labor until one’s health collapses, in stark contrast to the idea of

“free existence” implied in the statement.

J.J. Older adults have the right to access forms of study, apprenticeship, and work that are proportionate to their energy levels and freely chosen, and not to be compelled in any way to forms of forced rest.

The right to start living again

The right to “start living again” is often violated both in high-income countries and, even more severely, in countries with limited resources: older adults do not truly choose whether to study, work, or rest, but are pushed out of or kept in the workforce by structural barriers, ageism, and a lack of protections.

Where and how it is not respected

In many countries, mandatory retirement ages or forced retirement practices still exist, pushing older workers to leave the workforce regardless of their health, wishes, and abilities, turning “retirement” into an obligation rather than a choice. Even where the law no longer mandates retirement, corporate practices (pressure to

source_label_en: Charter of the Rights of Older Persons
title: Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection (part 9)
title_en: Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection (part 9)
text:
Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection

“step aside,” non-renewal of contracts, targeted reorganizations) effectively result in forced retirement, often without adequate income support.

In low- and middle-income countries, the violation takes the opposite but mirror-image form: the absence of pensions or their inadequacy forces many older adults to continue working in physically demanding and informal jobs, without any real possibility of “choosing” retirement.

Access to Education and Apprenticeships

The right to access education and apprenticeships is often disregarded because:

lifelong learning and continuing education systems primarily target younger, more skilled, and higher-income workers; older and less educated adults are systematically the ones who participate least in training;60

for older adults, practical and symbolic barriers compound: evening courses that are difficult to reach, enrollment costs, fear of “not making it” or of being judged, and the social perception of being “too old to study.”61

Recent studies show that older adults with low levels of education are at greater risk of leaving the workforce early and not returning, precisely because they lack access to retraining programs; in this way, the lack of access to education becomes a form of forced retirement, not a choice.

Specific barriers to “work commensurate with one’s energy”

With regard to “work proportionate to one’s energy and freely chosen,” the most evident violations are:

ageism in the workplace: stereotypes about older adults (less productive, less flexible, less

“technologically savvy”) lead to not hiring them, not promoting them, and not investing in their training, effectively making it impossible to find or keep a suitable job;62

poor job adaptation: few workplaces provide genuine accommodations (reduced physical workload, flexible hours, mentoring roles) that would allow people to continue working within their health and energy limits.

In some countries, policies to “raise the retirement age” have been introduced without changing actual working conditions or welfare systems

; the result is that many older workers leave the workforce anyway due to illness, burnout, or organizational conflicts, without having been able to choose either to work longer or to retire with dignity.

When rest becomes “forced”

The term “forced retirement” aptly describes what happens when:

the older worker is pushed out of the workforce (layoffs, non-renewal of contracts, mandatory retirement, informal pressure) without educational

or employment alternatives, and with insufficient pension

or welfare benefits;

an older adult who would like to engage in study, apprenticeships, skill-building volunteer work, or light work faces economic (costs), logistical (transportation, schedules), and cultural (feeling “out of place” among young people) barriers that confine them to unwanted inactivity.

source_label_en: Charter of the Rights of Older Persons
title: Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection (part 10)
title_en: Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection (part 10)
text:
Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection

The right is therefore far from being realized precisely where it is needed most: among the poor, poorly educated elderly with arduous and fragmented work histories, who are the most exposed both to forced labor under grueling conditions and to imposed inactivity without real opportunities for study, apprenticeships, and chosen work.

ł. Institutions have a duty to identify the elderly population as vulnerable and to enact legislation for their protection.

It is the duty of institutions to guarantee older adults forms of income support in cases of partial or total destitution or inadequate economic resources.

These two articles clearly identify a dual institutional duty: to recognize older adults as a vulnerable group and to provide income support mechanisms in cases of poverty or inadequate resources; the data show that this duty is only partially fulfilled, both in wealthy countries and in those with limited resources.

The idea that “older populations” should be identified as vulnerable is fully consistent with major international documents (UN, MIPPA, Council of Europe), which call on states to recognize older adults as a group exposed to specific risks (poverty, isolation, dependency, abuse) and to enact legislation for their protection.

This does not mean that every older person is frail, but that aging increases the likelihood of chronic illness, reduced income, and care needs

and discrimination, and therefore requires targeted regulations on income, housing, care, and legal and social protection.

The data show why “vulnerability” must be treated as a legal category and not merely a sociological one:

the World Social Protection Report notes that, globally, about half of older people do not receive any pension or old-age transfer, leaving them without a formal safety net;68

reports on older persons’ poverty highlight higher poverty rates among older people living alone, women, those in poor health, and ethnic minorities, revealing an internal stratification of vulnerability that legislation must explicitly address.

Income support in cases of poverty

The second article establishes a specific duty: to guarantee forms of income support for older adults living in poverty or with inadequate resources—that is, a genuine “floor” of minimum income in old age.

This logic underlies the non-contributory pensions and minimum income schemes for the elderly that several countries have introduced as the “zero pillar” of the pension system.

Comparative studies demonstrate the effectiveness of these instruments:

in Brazil and South Africa, non-contributory pensions significantly reduce poverty in households with at least one elderly person; one estimate shows a reduction in the “poverty headcount” of between 2. and 4. percentage points thanks to these transfers, with greater effects on the poorest households;72

source_label_en: Charter of the Rights of Older Persons
title: Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection (part 11)
title_en: Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection (part 11)
text:
Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection

In Europe, many countries combine minimum pensions with guaranteed income schemes for the elderly or top-up payments up to a certain threshold: for example, in Belgium, the “Income Guarantee for Older Persons” is fully funded by the state, provided either in addition to or in the absence of a contributory pension, indexed to inflation, and accompanied by additional benefits (subsidized rates, increased healthcare reimbursements).

It is the duty of institutions to ensure that health and social-health care and services are effectively provided free of charge.

This claim is largely contradicted by the data: in almost all countries, even where the healthcare system is “universal,” a significant portion of healthcare and social-healthcare costs still falls directly on the

and their families, to the point of causing impoverishment and the forgoing of care.

The duty to ensure the “effective free provision” of care reflects the principle of financial protection under universal health coverage: no one should have to choose between receiving care and maintaining a decent standard of living.

Effective free care means not only the absence of nominal copayments, but also the absence of out-of-pocket expenses that compromise daily life (medications, medical aids, transportation, home care, facility fees).

Data on “catastrophic” expenses

In Europe, up to 1 in 5 families experiences catastrophic health care costs (a very high proportion of their budget absorbed by health care expenses), particularly for medications, medical devices, and dental care, even in very wealthy countries.

Recent studies show that those facing catastrophic expenses have higher risks of mortality and worsening health, because they fall into poverty or forgo necessary further care.

The situation is even more critical for those with long-term needs: in 32 OECD/EU countries, out-of-pocket expenses for long-term care (LTC) can reach, on average, over 70% of the median income of older adults with severe needs, despite public assistance.

In nearly half of these countries, LTC costs are

close to or exceed the entire median income of the elderly person, effectively making necessary care “not free” and pushing many people into poverty or toward unmet care needs.

How the right is disregarded in practice

In high-income systems, copayments, deductibles, lists of excluded services, and cost-sharing for social and health care mean that “free” care exists on paper but not in people’s wallets: older adults pay for chronic medications, specialist visits, assistive devices (glasses, hearing aids, wheelchairs), and home care.

In long-term care, families often have to cover a large portion of the costs of nursing homes, caregivers, day centers, or home-based services; in OECD countries, nearly half of older adults with care needs are at risk of poverty precisely because of these expenses.

In resource-limited countries, this right is violated even more radically:

source_label_en: Charter of the Rights of Older Persons
title: Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection (part 12)
title_en: Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection (part 12)
text:
Charter, Art. 5 — The right to subsistence and income protection

the majority of healthcare spending is out-of-pocket, with no widespread insurance or public coverage, leading to significant forgoing of care, selling of assets, and indebtedness, especially among older adults with chronic illnesses.

Structured social and health services (home care, intermediate facilities, formal long-term care) are often absent or accessible only through private means; therefore, they effectively “do not exist” for the impoverished majority.

Specific Effects on Older Adults

Older adults are more likely to:

require frequent care, multiple medications, rehabilitation, and long-term care, increasing their exposure to copayments and out-of-pocket expenses compared to the rest of the population;

see their income or assets (pension, savings, home) eroded to pay for health and social-health care, to the point of having to forgo services, cut back on food or heating, or move to less suitable facilities because they are cheaper.

Studies on older adults in Europe indicate that high healthcare costs are associated not only with deteriorating health but also with social isolation and anxiety, because the fear of costs leads people to avoid check-ups, visits, or hospitalizations due to financial concerns.

In this context, the claim of “true free access” to health and social-healthcare services for older adults appears more like a distant goal than a fully realized right: health and long-term care (LTC) systems, as currently designed, still shift too high a share of the cost of care onto those who are most vulnerable.

109

title: Charter, Art. 6 — The Right to an Active Life (part 1)
title_en: Charter, Art. 6 — The Right to an Active Life (part 1)
text:
Charter, Art. 6 — The Right to an Active Life

The “right to an active life” means that older adults are not only entitled to care and protection, but also to continue—if they so desire and to the extent their condition allows—to participate in social, cultural, professional, political, and family life, rather than being pushed into forced passivity.

Active aging

Within the WHO framework, active aging is first and foremost the set of measures designed to prevent older adults from being excluded from the vital, cultural, social, and emotional circles of the community in which they live. It is also the process of optimizing opportunities for health, participation, and security to improve quality of life as people age.

Active living means:

maintaining, as far as possible, a good level of health and functional autonomy;

being able to participate in work, volunteer activities, study, culture, leisure, community life, and politics according to one’s desires and abilities;

feeling secure (economically, physically, and socially) and not forced into isolation or total dependence on others.

The following considerations and articles will partly revisit what has already been discussed above.

1. Older adults have the right to actively participate in social life, including through volunteer activities.

Loneliness, a global phenomenon

The articulation of this right to active participation—including through volunteer work—is a direct response to two intertwined processes: on the one hand, the loneliness and isolation of older adults resulting from their effective exclusion from society; on the other, the fragmentation of family and community networks, which has eroded social capital in many Western societies.

Loneliness, exclusion, and “expulsion” from society

Numerous studies show that a significant proportion

of older adults live alone and experience loneliness and isolation, not so much by choice as due to the cumulative effect of retirement, bereavement, loss of role, and barriers to participation. Recent meta-analyses estimate that about one-third of older adults worldwide experience forms of social isolation, and that the prevalence of loneliness among those over 60 is around 25–30%, with higher peaks in Central, Eastern, and Southern Europe.

This loneliness is not merely a “psychological” condition: the transition from dense social networks to lives marked by few contacts effectively represents a form of exclusion from the social fabric, a marginalization of older adults’ contributions. Research shows that increased isolation among those over 50 is associated with a higher risk of mortality, disability, and dementia, indicating that social exclusion has also become a powerful risk factor for health issues and functional decline.

Social fragmentation and the decline of social capital

source_label_en: Charter of the Rights of Older Persons
title: Charter, Art. 6 — The Right to an Active Life (part 2)
title_en: Charter, Art. 6 — The Right to an Active Life (part 2)
text:
Charter, Art. 6 — The Right to an Active Life

This phenomenon must be understood within a broader process: the shrinking of the family unit, the proliferation of small nuclear families or childless adults, the reduced stability of neighborhood networks, and the rise of individualism. Analyses of declining fertility and family changes in the West show that having fewer children and more childless adults reduces, over time, many forms of community participation,

weakening those neighborhood networks that constituted the “first line of defense” for the elderly.

In this context, older adults not only lose their role as the family “link” between generations, but often find themselves in societies where overall social capital—trust, civic participation, associative networks—is in decline. The result is twofold: fewer family ties to rely on and fewer organized communities in which to find a place, with a greater likelihood of social exclusion.

Volunteering as a response to loneliness and as a generator of social capital

In this scenario, the right to “actively participate in social life, including through volunteer activities” is much more than a mere detail: it is a mechanism to combat loneliness, isolation, and loss of role. International studies show that volunteering in old age improves psychological well-being, sense of purpose, perceived health, and, in some cases, is associated with lower mortality and reduced use of health services.

Volunteering by older adults should not, however, be understood as an individual therapy against loneliness, but rather as a genuine expression—as previously mentioned—of old age as an age of freedom and generosity, a powerful sign for other generations of how, even in the face of fragility and vulnerability—

, it is possible to care for others. Volunteering also represents one of the few remaining sources of social capital: it strengthens cohesion, trust, the community’s ability to respond to needs, and the creation of bonds between generations. The literature explicitly refers to older adults as bearers of human, social, and cultural capital which, when mobilized through volunteering, helps address collective challenges (education, care, the environment, support for the most vulnerable).

The right to participation as an antidote to “passivity” and marginalization

From this perspective, the article not only enshrines the freedom to volunteer but also the right not to be relegated to forced passivity, to the exclusive role of

“recipients of care.” To claim for the elderly the right to actively participate in social life means recognizing them as individuals still capable of giving, of cooperating, of building bonds—in a world where traditional social structures (extended family, parishes, mass organizations) have weakened.

Older Adults and Existing Volunteers

source_label_en: Charter of the Rights of Older Persons
title: Charter, Art. 6 — The Right to an Active Life (part 3)
title_en: Charter, Art. 6 — The Right to an Active Life (part 3)
text:
Charter, Art. 6 — The Right to an Active Life

In “aging” countries—where the proportion of the elderly population is high—the elderly are not merely potential volunteers: in many cases, they are already a central component of the world of organized volunteering and

informal sectors. Data show that, in several rapidly aging societies, those aged 60–65 have volunteer participation rates equal to or higher than those of other age groups, or in any case account for a very substantial portion of the total number of volunteer hours.99, 100

Europe: “Aged” Countries with a High Presence of Older Volunteers

A comparative analysis of senior volunteering in Europe indicates that, in countries such as the Netherlands, Finland, Germany, and the United Kingdom, the proportion of older adults engaged in volunteering is high and often growing.

In the Netherlands, approximately 41% of people aged 65 to 74 and 24% of those over 75 participate in volunteer activities; in Finland, the figure is around 40% for those aged 65 to 79.

In Germany, the volunteering rate is 37% among those aged 60–69 and 25% among those over 70; in the United Kingdom, approximately 30% of those aged 65–74 and 20% of those over 75 engage in volunteer activities.

In Italy, too, participation by older adults in labor unions or volunteer activities such as the Food Bank or the Pharmaceutical Bank is very high.

These are precisely “aging” countries in a demographic sense—with high proportions of people over 65—where older adults represent a visible and recognized pillar of the volunteer sector, from associations of

welfare associations to cultural, sports, educational, and religious services.

OECD Data and the Role of Unpaid Volunteering by Older Adults

An OECD report on unpaid work among older adults shows that people aged 65 and over engage in volunteering more often than young people and middle-aged workers, although they spend slightly fewer minutes per day on it among those who already volunteer. On average, in OECD countries, older adults spend a total amount of time on unpaid work (care, household chores, volunteering) comparable to that of working-age adults, but with a higher proportion devoted to volunteering and civic activities.

This means that, in countries where the population over 65 has already exceeded 20%, a significant portion of social cohesion—from neighborhood associations to charitable organizations—effectively relies on an “army” of older volunteers. If this contribution were monetized in terms of equivalent services, the economic value would be significant and largely underestimated in national accounts.

2. Older adults have the right to access cultural and recreational services, as well as to...

express their thoughts and to broaden their cultural horizons, even in the presence of physical and mental limitations.

§ 3. Older adults have the right to access educational, apprenticeship, and training programs in accordance with their interests and in line with the principles of active aging.

source_label_en: Charter of the Rights of Older Persons
title: Charter, Art. 6 — The Right to an Active Life (part 4)
title_en: Charter, Art. 6 — The Right to an Active Life (part 4)
text:
Charter, Art. 6 — The Right to an Active Life

§4. Society has a duty to prevent all forms of exclusion and to promote effective integration into educational and training settings.

Older Adults and Culture

Access to culture and education in old age is not a treatment or a remedy, but a fundamental right of the person, rooted in the very idea of humanity and dignity at all stages of life. Study, cultural participation, and the opportunity to express one’s thoughts do not serve merely to “prevent” something, but are ways through which older adults continue to exercise freedom, creativity, memory, and responsibility toward others.

Culture as an Expression of the Person

Research on lifelong learning in old age shows that learning, reading, and participating in artistic and civic activities allow older adults to remain thinking individuals, capable of questioning the present, transmitting knowledge, and reinterpreting their own history. Speaking of culture as “therapy” would reverse the relationship: the elderly person would appear as a patient in need of correction, whereas they are, in fact, a protagonist of cultural and civic life, with their own original and irreplaceable contribution.

Social effects without functional reductionism

It is true that the cultural participation of older adults produces positive effects on the relational and social levels: it strengthens social capital, counteracts social isolation, fosters intergenerational encounters, and sustains the life of cultural institutions. However, these effects must be recognized as an expression of the potential of older adults, not as the sole reason for the existence of this right: culture is due to the older person because they remain, until the end, a subject of speech, thought, and the creation of meaning, and because, from this perspective, they make an effective contribution to society.

It is society’s duty to guarantee services for digital inclusion, e-learning, and easy-

learning through IT tools.

The prospect of digital inclusion is crucial but ambivalent. On the one hand, e-learning and ICT tools open up new possibilities for older adults with limited mobility, time constraints, or distance barriers: online courses, reading groups, telemedicine, and access to cultural services and content. Studies on e-learning in older age show that, when well-designed, online learning can foster social integration, maintain skills, and reduce isolation.

On the other hand, European data indicate a still-enormous digital divide: nearly half of those over 65 in the EU have never used the Internet, and only 1 in 4 among those aged 65–74 possesses basic digital skills. This means that if cultural, educational, and public services become “digital by default” without adequate safeguards, there is a risk of replacing analog exclusion with a new form of digital exclusion among older adults. For this reason, alongside the right to e-learning and the use

of IT tools, it would be important to emphasize at least three limits/conditions:122

source_label_en: Charter of the Rights of Older Persons
title: Charter, Art. 6 — The Right to an Active Life (part 5)
title_en: Charter, Art. 6 — The Right to an Active Life (part 5)
text:
Charter, Art. 6 — The Right to an Active Life

the obligation to maintain analog channels for essential services, so that no one is deprived of their rights due to a lack of digital skills;123

the need for digital literacy programs specifically designed for older adults, with personalized support, a slow pace, and intergenerational mentoring;124

the obligation to design age-friendly platforms and content (accessibility, simplicity, readability), involving older adults themselves in the design of digital services.

In this way, Articles 6.2–6. do not remain an abstract declaration, but define a true social pact: to guarantee older people the opportunity to continue thinking, learning, and expressing themselves, including through digital means, without digital technology becoming a new tool of exclusion.

120

source_label_en: Charter of the Rights of Older Persons
title: Charter, Art. 7 — The right to a safe living space (part 1)
title_en: Charter, Art. 7 — The right to a safe living space (part 1)
text:
Charter, Art. 7 — The right to a safe living space

Older adults have the right to live in safe living spaces that are adaptable to their personal preferences and abilities.

Society has a duty to monitor the safety conditions of such environments and to ensure their habitability and minimum comfort.

In many countries, the right of older adults to live in safe, adaptable living spaces monitored by society is largely denied: millions of older adults live in cold, unsanitary, inaccessible, and unsafe homes, often without any systematic monitoring of their living conditions.

Unsafe, cold, and dilapidated homes

In the United Kingdom, a 2024–2025 study shows that more than 1 in 5 older adults lives in homes with serious problems (dampness, leaks, cold, structural defects), and that among the approximately 4. million people over 50

with conditions exacerbated by the cold, 1 in 3 lives in homes with at least one serious housing problem.

Among people aged 50 and over with health problems, 15% report three or more serious housing defects; older adults who rent and those from ethnic minorities are the most affected: up to 46% of people over 50 of Black, Asian, and Minority Ethnic (BAME) origin live in homes with at least one significant housing problem.

International studies directly link these conditions to worsening respiratory, cardiovascular, and musculoskeletal conditions in older adults, leading to increased hospitalizations, emergency room visits, and winter mortality.

Home Safety and the Risk of Falls

An analysis of a representative sample of

2,599 older adults in the United States (Medicare beneficiaries, age 65+) estimates that in 2019, 34.7% experienced at least one fall in a year; the presence of home disorders (clutter, obstructions, problematic home conditions) is associated with a significant increase in the risk of falling compared to homes without such issues.

Studies of older populations in Asia show that more than half of falls occur at home, often due to slippery floors, poor lighting, steep stairs, unsafe bathrooms, and the absence of handrails or grab bars.

These data show that many home environments are neither “safe” nor adapted to reduced motor abilities, violating the right set forth in Art.

7. and increasing the risk of disability, loss of autonomy, and institutionalization.

Adaptability and accessibility: a minority of “age-friendly” homes

In England, only about 10% of older households live in specialized housing or homes designed for older adults; the vast majority of older adults live in “normal” homes, often built decades ago, which are ill-suited to mobility or sensory limitations.

Studies on age-friendly housing show that the demand for adaptable housing far exceeds the supply; economic barriers (renovation costs), informational barriers (lack of awareness of available options), and bureaucratic barriers hinder modifications (ramps, elevators, adapted bathrooms, removal of barriers).

source_label_en: Charter of the Rights of Older Persons
title: Charter, Art. 7 — The right to a safe living space (part 2)
title_en: Charter, Art. 7 — The right to a safe living space (part 2)
text:
Charter, Art. 7 — The right to a safe living space

Longitudinal studies indicate, however, that targeted adaptations (grab bars, bathroom modifications, elimination of steps) can slow the decline in independence in daily activities and reduce the likelihood of falls among older adults with mobility issues, confirming that housing adaptability is a key factor for a dignified life at home.

Monitoring obligation: what is not happening

Article 7. requires society to monitor safety, habitability, and minimum comfort; in practice:

many countries lack systematic systems to monitor the housing conditions of older adults living in private homes: interventions often occur only after incidents (falls, fires, hospitalizations) or upon reporting, not as preventive monitoring;139

older adults in social housing or private rentals are often “forgotten”: a 2024 study on older adults in social housing highlights a combination of poverty, poor housing conditions, and unmet health needs, with heavy reliance on emergency services; The authors refer to a “systemically vulnerable” population whose housing conditions are neither adequately monitored nor managed.

Globally, reports from the UN and organizations such as HelpAge indicate:

in many low- and middle-income countries, older adults live in slums, informal settlements, overcrowded homes, or structurally unsafe dwellings, without minimum regulated standards of habitability (ventilation, structural soundness, sanitation);141

the absence of regular inspections, adequate housing programs for older adults, and age-friendly city policies means that older adults’ housing quality depends almost entirely on household income, not on a guaranteed right.

There are no precise global estimates specifically for older adults living in slums, but available data suggest that we are talking about many millions of people, concentrated mainly in the major cities of sub-Saharan Africa, South and East Asia, and parts of Latin America, often in settlements lacking safe water, reliable electricity, and adequate sanitation.

How many older adults live in slums?

In 2022, over 1.1–1. billion people lived in informal settlements or slums, about 30% of the urban population in developing countries; the majority are in sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Southeast Asia.

In sub-Saharan Africa, about 55% of urban residents live in slums; this region also has the fastest-growing urban elderly population, so the proportion of people over 60 in slums is rising sharply.

In less developed countries, the population aged 65 and older averages about 3.7% of the total, but is growing rapidly; in cities, the proportion of older adults tends to be slightly lower, but is rising rapidly.

If we conservatively estimate that at least 3–5% of the world’s slum dwellers are older adults (60+), we are already talking about

35–60 million older adults living in informal settlements, many of whom:147

without running water in their homes;

with shared or unsafe latrines;

source_label_en: Charter of the Rights of Older Persons
title: Charter, Art. 7 — The right to a safe living space (part 3)
title_en: Charter, Art. 7 — The right to a safe living space (part 3)
text:
Charter, Art. 7 — The right to a safe living space

with irregular or no electrical connections.

Comparative analyses of poverty among the elderly in African slums indicate that:148

most elderly slum-dwellers experience food insecurity and “absolute asset deprivation” (no assets to sell, no savings);

the combination of being over 60 years old and living in a slum is associated with very high levels of material deprivation and insufficient access to basic services, including water and sanitation.

Older adults have the right to live in their own homes for as long as possible, and society has a duty to provide protective, preventive, and home care services, including through the use of telemedicine.

Article 7. formalizes one of the most critical issues in aging policies: the right

to remain in one’s own home for as long as possible, and society’s corresponding duty to build a genuine infrastructure of protection, prevention, home care, and telemedicine around the home. Today, this right is largely disregarded both in developed countries and, even more dramatically, in countries with limited resources.

Global shortage of home care services

Globally, more than 142 million older adults have functional limitations that require assistance with daily activities, and the majority live in lower- and middle-income countries, where there is no structured long-term care system. In many contexts, care is left almost entirely to families—especially women—without home care services, professional support, or telemedicine, with the result that millions of older adults do not receive adequate care and cannot remain at home in dignified conditions. The WHO and various international organizations report that the political priority given to long-term care remains low, and that most countries have neither a national plan for home care nor minimum standards for universal access. In fact, the “right to live at home for as long as possible” is often left to the economic and organizational capabilities of individual families, rather than being guaranteed

as a social right.

A right that requires a revolution in care systems

In summary, Article 7. calls for a genuine transformation of long-term care systems: 153

in developed countries, shifting resources and priorities from institutional care to home-based and community care, integrating telemedicine and prevention;

in resource-limited countries, establishing for the first time a minimal but universal network of home-based services and caregiver support, so that

“staying at home” does not equate to abandonment.

Only in this way does the right to live in one’s own home “as long as possible” cease to be a rhetorical formula and become an operational criterion for redesigning elder care in the 21st century.

Developed countries: imbalance between institutional and home-based care

source_label_en: Charter of the Rights of Older Persons
title: Charter, Art. 7 — The right to a safe living space (part 4)
title_en: Charter, Art. 7 — The right to a safe living space (part 4)
text:
Charter, Art. 7 — The right to a safe living space

In advanced economies, the picture is more complex: home-based services exist, but they are often underfunded, fragmented, and difficult to access. In many European countries, the European Commission notes that home-based and community services are the weakest link in long-term care systems: well-developed in the Nordic countries, but limited or highly unequal in Southern and Eastern Europe.

As a result, many older adults enter residential facilities prematurely or remain at home, placing an enormous burden on families and with little professional support, despite policies that state the goal of promoting aging in place. Even telemedicine, which saw explosive growth during the pandemic, remains largely inaccessible to many older adults, hindered by digital divides, technological barriers, operator concerns, and a lack of stable funding models.

Countries with limited resources: homes without services, overburdened families

In low- and middle-income countries, the problem is different but mirror-image: the norm is to remain at home, but often without any formalized home care services. Care is almost entirely provided by family members, in contexts of poverty, rapid urbanization, and unsuitable housing, with very little access to home visits, rehabilitation, assistive devices, telemedicine, or support for caregivers. This situation effectively violates the stated right: simply “not being in an institution” is not enough to say that one lives at home with dignity; without services, the elderly person risks neglect, abuse, and lack of access to basic care. Furthermore, the absence of formal long-term care (LTC) systems for the elderly limits the education and employment opportunities of younger women, who must compensate by providing unpaid care, thereby perpetuating cycles of poverty.

Benefits of Home Care Compared to Residential Care

Comparative literature shows that, when well-organized, home care offers significant advantages over institutionalization, both on a human and economic level.

Systematic reviews indicate that “home with support” programs (home care provided by multidisciplinary teams) reduce hospitalizations, admissions to facilities, and falls, while improving functional ability and, in some cases, survival compared to independent living without support alone.

Some studies suggest that, for many older adults, home care is more cost-effective than residential long-term care, despite requiring initial investments in staff and coordination.

Recent analyses in China show that, for individuals with similar needs, home-based care promotes greater social participation, better mental and physical health, and is more economically sustainable for families and public systems, while institutional care tends to be more expensive and, if lacking in social interaction, can impair autonomy and cognitive function.

title: Charter, Art. 7 — The right to a safe living space (part 5)
title_en: Charter, Art. 7 — The right to a safe living space (part 5)
text:
Charter, Art. 7 — The right to a safe living space

These data confirm that helping older adults remain in their own homes as long as possible, with adequate preventive, protective, and care services, is not only a humanly preferable choice but often also

more efficient and sustainable than early transfers to facilities.

Telemedicine: Opportunities and Limitations

The explicit reference to telemedicine is highly relevant. Telehealth can:163

facilitate the management of chronic conditions, reducing the need for travel and unnecessary hospital visits;

improve monitoring, treatment adherence, and communication among older adults, caregivers, and services.

However, studies highlight that many older adults face significant barriers: lack of access to internet connections and devices, low digital literacy, sensory or cognitive difficulties, and even implicit biases among healthcare providers who hesitate to offer telemedicine visits to older adults. Without targeted strategies (training, simplified devices, in-person support, hybrid channels), there is a risk that telemedicine will become a new factor of exclusion.

It appears crucial that telemedicine networks be integrated into service networks consisting of home care providers who are always available, connected through physical coordination and control centers, and equipped with the necessary mobility for timely and precise interventions. Telemedicine without human support creates further distances.

In the event of the loss or unavailability of their home, older adults have the right to access appropriate financial assistance to secure adequate housing.

Article 7. recognizes that older adults not only have the right not to be evicted, but also to have access—even after losing or lacking a home—to adequate housing through specific financial assistance. This is crucial in a context where, even in Europe, a significant proportion of older adults experience housing insecurity: difficulty paying rent or utilities, cold or unsanitary homes, risk of eviction, or forced cohabitation.

In developed countries, the picture is paradoxical: many older adults live in under-occupied housing (nearly half of those over 65 in the EU live in homes that are “too large” for their household), yet a significant portion struggles to cover housing costs or lives in conditions of material deprivation (homes not adequately heated, structural deficiencies). In resource-limited countries, the problem is even more acute: millions of older adults live in shanties, informal settlements, or precarious housing, without water, heating, or sanitation, and with no protection against losing their homes due to debt, conflict, or disasters.

title: Charter, Art. 7 — The right to a safe living space (part 6)
title_en: Charter, Art. 7 — The right to a safe living space (part 6)
text:
Charter, Art. 7 — The right to a safe living space

In small towns, especially in inland areas, older adults remain among the few permanent residents, often in old homes that are too large and difficult to heat and maintain. Depopulation creates a paradox: many empty homes, yet poor older adults who are unable to adapt or maintain their own homes, increasing the risk of isolation, household accidents, and energy poverty. From this perspective, economic incentives are not merely individual subsidies but a tool of territorial policy: renovating, adapting, and facilitating access to housing for the elderly in small towns also means combating depopulation and giving new purpose to the built environment.

7.J. It is the duty of institutions to guarantee older adults adequate services in light of specific physical and health conditions or the existence of architectural barriers.

Article 7. is even more decisive: it does not merely speak of housing, but affirms the duty of institutions to guarantee adequate services in the presence of particular physical and health conditions or architectural barriers. In practice, it requires rethinking the elderly person’s home as a node in a network of services: structural adaptations (ramps, elevators, accessible bathrooms), assistance

, transportation, home-based health and social services, and community support.

In developed countries, research shows that older adults in rural areas and small towns face greater difficulties: fewer transportation services, less structured home care, fewer healthcare facilities, and more barriers in the built environment and daily routines. Age-friendly communities in rural settings are created precisely to address this: adapting homes, public spaces, and local services to the needs of a large and often impoverished older population.

In resource-limited countries, the deficit is twofold: there is a lack of both physical adaptations (homes that are often unsafe and lacking essential services) and a network of support services, with entire rural areas becoming “service deserts” for older adults and people with disabilities. Here, Article 7. calls for global territorial justice: it is not enough to guarantee rights in large cities; it is necessary to ensure that villages, rural outskirts, and small towns also have basic services to allow older adults to remain safely in their homes.

Housing, small municipalities, and depopulation: a structural link

The connection between these articles, small municipalities, and depopulation is strong:174

Depopulation drives away young people, jobs, and services, leaving older adults alone in old, often unsuitable homes, with fewer shops, less transportation, and fewer healthcare facilities;

the presence of older adults without adequate support makes these areas even less attractive, fueling the cycle of demographic decline, school closures, shop closures, service closures, and further out-migration. Recognizing the right to adequate housing (7.4)

source_label_en: Charter of the Rights of Older Persons
title: Charter, Art. 7 — The right to a safe living space (part 7)
title_en: Charter, Art. 7 — The right to a safe living space (part 7)
text:
Charter, Art. 7 — The right to a safe living space

and the duty to provide services and adaptations (7.5) means, in reality, proposing a strategy to combat depopulation: housing programs for the elderly, cohousing, renovation of the housing stock, and community care services can become the driving force behind a new life in small towns, also attracting families, service providers, and forms of the social economy. International experiences with age-friendly rural and remote communities show that investing in housing for the elderly—home adaptations, neighborhood services, transportation, and tele-services—improves quality of life, reduces the need to move to cities or care facilities, and keeps community ties alive.

In this light, 7. and 7. are not merely technical provisions on housing, but a genuine policy agenda: placing the home and the needs of older adults at the center of strategies for regions facing demographic decline, transforming aging from a factor of abandonment into an opportunity for social and urban regeneration, especially in small towns.

7.1. Society has a duty to promote and encourage forms of supportive cohousing that allow older adults, where they so desire, to find a familiar, welcoming environment that provides concrete assistance in managing daily life.

Poverty and Precarity in Countries with Limited Resources

In low- and middle-income countries, the picture is different: older adults more often live in extended families, but under conditions of poverty and precariousness.

Multidimensional poverty among the elderly is concentrated in low-income countries: on average, about one-third of those over 60 are poor in this sense, facing deficiencies in income, housing, health, nutrition, and education. Many older adults live in overcrowded, informal housing without services, or in households under severe economic stress, where traditional solidarity is

no longer able to guarantee care and security.

Here the problem is not so much the single-person household as the fragility of the support network: children who have migrated, dependent grandchildren, unstable incomes, and the absence of pensions or social protections. For many poor older adults, “living with family” does not automatically mean receiving care, time, or a listening ear, but often means sharing scarce resources and the struggles of survival.

Still on the topic of cohousing: elderly people living alone and single-person households in wealthy countries

In wealthy countries, a very high proportion of older adults live alone and experience loneliness.

A meta-analysis of high-income countries estimates that approximately 28–30% of people over 60 experience loneliness, at least to some extent.

International data on living arrangements show that, in many OECD countries, older adults are the most represented age group in single-person households: the proportion of people over 65 living alone ranges from less than 10% in some Eastern European countries to nearly 50% in others (e.g., Lithuania).

title: Charter, Art. 8 — The right to a social life (part 1)
title_en: Charter, Art. 8 — The right to a social life (part 1)
text:
Charter, Art. 8 — The right to a social life

Older adults have the right to an active social life

The right to an active life applies to all older adults, even when they have severe physical or cognitive limitations. In this sense, “active” does not mean only work, sports, or functional independence, but above all the opportunity to form relationships, express emotions, and participate—according to one’s abilities—in emotional, spiritual, and community life. Even those who are bedridden, no longer walk, or have advanced dementia retain the right to conversation, to listening, to human contact, to prayer, or to other forms of inner nourishment.

For this reason, the statement “The elderly person has the right to an active social life” must be understood in the most inclusive sense possible. A person in a wheelchair can lead an active life through visits from family and friends, phone calls or video calls, groups

reading or prayer groups in the ward or in a nursing home; an elderly person with aphasia can participate through eye contact, gestures, singing, or listening to music or sacred texts; those with severe dementia can still benefit from a presence by their bedside, a hand held, and simple, familiar words. An active life, in this context, means that no one is reduced to “just a body to be cared for,” but remains a person capable of relationships, with the right to be involved, listened to, and accompanied in a respectful and personalized way.

The elderly person has the right to live with whomever they choose.

The key point here is relational freedom: the elderly person must not be automatically “assigned” to an unwanted living arrangement (whether family-based or institutional). Studies on families and living arrangements show that the quality of the bond—not just the physical presence of someone—is crucial for mental and cognitive well-being: emotional support from adult children and partners is associated with a lower risk of depression and cognitive decline. The right to live with whomever one chooses therefore includes: chosen living arrangements with children, partners, friends, cohousing, religious or secular communities. But above all, it protects against being placed

in institutions or “forced” domestic situations, which are often perceived as hostile or violent.

Institutions and society have a duty to avoid, with regard to older adults, any form of confinement, ghettoization, or isolation that prevents them from interacting freely with people of all age groups in the population.

source_label_en: Charter of the Rights of Older Persons
title: Charter, Art. 8 — The right to a social life (part 2)
title_en: Charter, Art. 8 — The right to a social life (part 2)
text:
Charter, Art. 8 — The right to a social life

The experience of COVID-19 restrictions has dramatically demonstrated what it means to violate this article: studies on nursing homes document that prolonged closures, room confinement, and visitation bans have led to loss of mobility, reduced independence, weight loss, worsening mood, anxiety, and disorientation, especially among people with dementia. In several countries, the total suspension of visits has been recognized as a severe infringement of the right to self-determination and emotional well-being, with “side effects” on health that are often not offset by benefits in terms of infection control.

Ghettoization is not limited to care facilities: age-based segregation in neighborhoods, services, and activities (“seniors-only” spaces) can reduce opportunities for

contact with other generations, fueling mutual stereotypes. Data on intergenerational contact show that the reduction of mixed-age spaces (schools open to the neighborhood, community centers, intergenerational projects) harms not only older adults but also young people, who develop greater anxiety about aging and more prejudices.

It is the duty of institutions to ensure support for households that include older adults and that wish to continue living together.

A point that has not been made explicit so far is that the “right to live with whomever one wishes” is largely conditioned by families’ ability to sustain cohabitation. In Europe, long-term care protection increasingly relies on three instruments: services, cash transfers to the elderly person, and support measures for family caregivers. Cash-for-care schemes (care allowances, Pflegegeld, etc.) and other forms of financial support are often valued precisely because they allow families to organize living arrangements, reduce working hours, or pay for help, although there are significant differences in generosity and equity across countries.

Two factors must be kept in mind:

without leave, work flexibility, tax breaks, and respite services, living together risks becoming an overwhelming burden for family members (especially women), with negative effects on health, income, and career; this is because, in all OECD countries, the majority of unpaid care hours continue to fall on women, who often have more precarious and part-time careers, and a strong internalization of “natural” caregiving roles;8

Support for households must not serve merely to “save” on institutional long-term care, but to make the choice to live together truly free and sustainable, preventing families from becoming the

“safety net” that absorbs all the shortcomings of the system.

8.J. Institutions and society have a duty to ensure the emotional continuity of older adults through visits, contact, and interaction with their relatives or with those with whom they have emotional relationships.

This article, 8.5, may specifically address the continuity of relationships during hospital stays, periods in care facilities, and health emergencies.

title: Charter, Art. 8 — The right to a social life (part 3)
title_en: Charter, Art. 8 — The right to a social life (part 3)
text:
Charter, Art. 8 — The right to a social life

Research on visitation restrictions in nursing homes and hospitals during the pandemic has revealed:0

a deterioration in the emotional well-being of older adults, feelings of abandonment, and a loss of meaning in daily routines;

suffering also for family members (anxiety, guilt, difficulty in making care decisions), with a breakdown of the trust between families and services.

It is interesting to note that some experiences have demonstrated the possibility of combining visits with safety measures (testing, dedicated areas, protective protocols) without eliminating contact entirely, suggesting that an absolute ban was not the only option. Looking ahead, this reinforces the idea that the right to emotional relationships—visits, contact, social interaction—should be considered a fundamental right, to be restricted only in a strictly proportionate and temporary manner, not an expendable organizational variable.

The possibility of an active social life is not guaranteed not only in cases where people are confined to their homes or care facilities, with limited opportunities for meetings and visits, but also when care facilities are separated from neighborhood life.

Therefore, the commitment of institutions and communities must be to foster, at every level, a fruitful relationship between young and old and to encourage diverse forms of integration.

Aurelia is 85 years old and has been living in a nursing home in the heart of a densely populated neighborhood in Rome for the past five years. She has a very active social life. Every day she visits her friends, goes shopping, and has long conversations with the local shopkeepers who know her, or pays a visit to her doctor, who has also become a trusted confidant. Then the pandemic hits and the facility’s doors close: no one is allowed to leave. Even after the period of strictest restrictions on movement has passed, residents still cannot leave the facility. Anyone who leaves cannot return. Aurelia feels overwhelmed by this situation, but she is aware of the global emergency and the tragedy that has upended so many lives. She complains a little but tries to persevere, waiting to see the end of this terrible epidemic. But with the new wave of the pandemic, the virus also enters the nursing home where she lives: almost all the elderly residents and the elderly nuns in the home fall ill. At one point, Aurelia also tests positive for Covid, but fortunately she manages to overcome the illness without having to be hospitalized. Other residents of the facility, along with the nuns, are forced to be hospitalized, and some never return. Six of them die.

Aurelia is devastated. When, before the summer,

infections began to decline and restrictions to ease, she asked to be allowed to go out: after all, all Italian citizens are permitted to leave their homes and move about freely.

She is repeatedly told that she is not allowed to leave, that once she leaves, she will not be able to return. So, after a few days, she packs her bags, books a room at a bed and breakfast, and walks out the door of the facility to reclaim her lost freedom. She made it.

title: Charter, Art. 9 — The right to freedom of movement (part 1)
title_en: Charter, Art. 9 — The right to freedom of movement (part 1)
text:
Charter, Art. 9 — The right to freedom of movement

Older adults have the right to move freely and to travel.

Institutions have a duty to take measures to facilitate the mobility of older adults and ensure adequate access to infrastructure designed for them.

A huge proportion of older adults worldwide are currently unable to truly exercise their right to move freely, even though they wish to do so: data show that mobility limitations are one of the earliest and most widespread forms of loss of autonomy in old age. Institutions, especially in rural, outlying, or low-income areas, are still far from ensuring adequate transportation and infrastructure, with consequences for health, participation, and fundamental rights.

International studies indicate that about one-third of people aged 70 and the majority of those over 85 report mobility limitations (walking, doing

1–3

stairs, moving around their neighborhood). In China, for example, a large national survey estimates a prevalence of mobility limitations of 30.4% among older adults living in the community, with an annual incidence of new cases of 18.1%.

A recent systematic review shows that difficulties are not limited to outdoor settings: many older adults also report significant challenges with indoor mobility (fatigue, loss of balance, barriers in the home environment, weakness), with reduced independence even for short trips within the home.6, 17 These limitations are associated with an increased risk of falls, hospitalizations, reduced quality of life, and increased mortality, indicating that freedom of movement is one of the central determinants of health in old age.

Transportation and Infrastructure Barriers: Data and Challenges

Outdoor mobility depends largely on access to adequate transportation and usable public spaces.

In Europe, a review of older adults’ transportation needs highlights four major barriers: physical accessibility (stairs, sidewalks, boarding buses and trains), service availability and frequency, costs, and a lack of clear and usable information. It is estimated that between 10% and 20% of European citizens—including many older adults—still face significant barriers to accessing public transportation, despite decades of accessibility policies.

In rural and non-urban areas, recent studies show that older adults cite limited schedules, overly restricted service areas, difficulties getting on and off vehicles, the need for complex reservations, and the lack of door-to-door services as the main obstacles. Where transportation is scarce or inadequate, the consequences are tangible: more missed or postponed medical appointments, reduced access to healthy food, and fewer opportunities to participate in social, cultural, and religious life. U.S. analyses, for example, directly link transportation barriers to an increase in avoidable emergency room visits and hospitalizations among seniors; when age-friendly transportation services and specific benefits are introduced, a reduction of up to 40% in emergency room visits

title: Charter, Art. 9 — The right to freedom of movement (part 2)
title_en: Charter, Art. 9 — The right to freedom of movement (part 2)
text:

for certain older populations.

The data suggest at least three concrete approaches to fulfilling the institutional duty referred to in 9.2:3

age-friendly public transportation: low-floor buses and trains, ramps, priority seating that is actually available, nearby and safe stops, clear and legible information, schedules coordinated with health and social services;4

policies for complete streets and active transportation: continuous, obstacle-free sidewalks, safe crossings, adequate lighting, and benches for resting, enabling older adults to walk and use mobility aids safely, not just “reach the stop”;5

tailored services for rural and vulnerable areas: on-demand transportation, organized volunteer services, vouchers or subsidies for essential travel (healthcare, shopping, social visits), as indicated by studies on age-friendly rural communities.

From this perspective, Articles 9. and 9. do not merely reaffirm freedom of movement as an abstract principle, but call on decision-makers to measure the quality of aging based on a simple indicator: how many older adults can actually leave their homes, get around, use public transportation, and travel safely. Where this does not happen, the limitation is not only “clinical” but also a sign that infrastructure and policies have not yet lived up to this right.

title: Charter, Art. 10 — The right to choose care and the right to appropriate care
title_en: Charter, Art. 10 — The right to choose care and the right to appropriate care
text:
Charter, Art. 10 — The right to choose care and the right to appropriate care

Older adults have the right to participate in determining care pathways and types of treatment, and to choose how health and social-health care is provided.

Healthcare and social-healthcare institutions and providers have a duty to present older adults with all available alternatives for the provision of healthcare and social-healthcare services.

The exercise of this right is not facilitated by the various choices—which are not always appropriate—made regarding healthcare and social-healthcare services. For example, if the patient chooses to remain at home rather than seek admission to social-healthcare facilities, all healthcare costs must be borne by the patient or their family, given the insufficient supply of services

of home-based and integrated healthcare services. It appears desirable—if not necessary—for public institutions to make a financial commitment aimed at ensuring freedom and equality of choice among the various forms of healthcare and social-healthcare services.

The choice of care setting must be made in accordance with the wishes of the elderly person receiving care, and in line with their needs and financial resources. Cases of abuse are not uncommon, such as the practice of transferring elderly people who require rehabilitative care to post-acute and long-term care wards, a transfer often carried out without the consent of the person concerned.

The elderly person has the right to informed consent regarding medical treatments, as provided for by current legislation.

Older adults have the right to high-quality care and treatments tailored to their personal needs and wishes.

10.J. Older adults have the right to appropriate and effective access to all healthcare services deemed necessary in relation to their health status.

10.ł. Older adults have the right to be cared for and treated in the environment that best ensures the recovery of impaired function.

Much has been said on these topics in the preceding sections, to which reference is made.

title: Charter, Art. 12 — The right to companionship and human connection (part 1)
title_en: Charter, Art. 12 — The right to companionship and human connection (part 1)
text:
Charter, Art. 12 — The right to companionship and human connection

Every older adult has the right to be accompanied, listened to, and supported at the end of life.

Accompaniment is a fundamental aspect of the care relationship: it expresses an attitude of acceptance and solidarity toward the sick person, which also underlies clinical practice in its various operational forms. More generally, it is a disposition to be considered a defining feature of any human relationship lived responsibly. Accompaniment becomes particularly arduous and complex as death approaches: it involves “knowing how to be present” (to stay), keeping vigil with those suffering the anguish of dying, “consoling”—that is, being-with in solitude, being a presence that opens the way to hope. The first step, which stems from the fundamental need to place the sick person at the center, is attentive and open-minded listening to the questions—often very uncomfortable ones—that arise in this most delicate phase of life. Even those who...

is confronted with fundamental questions in which they find themselves implicated and for which they are often unprepared: becoming a neighbor and remaining close to those who see death approaching leads to questioning oneself as well. The caregiver is confronted with the same questions experienced by the person being cared for: the meaning of life and suffering, dignity, loneliness, the fear of being abandoned, and, at times, even the request to end one’s life. The latter is a question with many implications, evoking guilt, shame, pain, helplessness, and the desire not to lose control. The interplay of projections between the patient and the caregiver is highly complex: distinguishing between “they are suffering too much” and “I am suffering too much (seeing them this way)” is by no means easy, just as it is very challenging to take seriously the request for a relationship that helps one navigate the profound loneliness of dying. Sincere and personalized communication, tailored to the capacity and willingness each person expresses to receive and to be able to process (cognitively and emotionally) information regarding their health and the progression of the illness, is part of this journey and strengthens the relationship. At times, this involves overcoming a reluctance that—perhaps disguised as respect for the other—masks a fear of being inadequate and a lack of sensitivity in listening, an inability to modulate not only the “what” and the “how much” to say, always respecting the person’s autonomy

and their right to “know,” but also the “how.”

From this perspective, accompanying the terminally ill patient is a true therapeutic act, fully integrated into the practice of care. As the literature on palliative care* reminds us, accompaniment shifts the therapeutic focus from healing to caring and allows for care when healing is not possible, directing the intervention toward the relief of overall suffering, the protection of dignity, and the support of hope for the patient and their family members.

title: Charter, Art. 12 — The right to companionship and human connection (part 2)
title_en: Charter, Art. 12 — The right to companionship and human connection (part 2)
text:
Charter, Art. 12 — The right to companionship and human connection

Society must guarantee a supportive presence, comfort, and respect for their spiritual, relational, and existential needs.

This article describes a very serious gap between need and response. What is described does not happen when:

the person is left alone for long periods, with limited or no visits, and experiences a sense of isolation and abandonment, which increases anxiety, vulnerability, and despair;

spiritual needs (meaning, forgiveness, reconciliation-

Fact Sheet, Geneva, World Health Organization, 2020.

(spirituality, inner peace) are neither heard nor mentioned: the presence remains merely technical, not truly supportive;

no structured spiritual/relational support is provided: there is a lack of trained personnel (spiritual care providers, counselors, trained volunteers), so no one has the explicit responsibility to address the inner experiences of the patient and the family;*

the organization limits or hinders the presence of family members (strict visiting rules, closed wards, lack of flexibility), leading to a deterioration in the mental health, the quality of relationships, and the sense of autonomy of the vulnerable person;

staff members, who are overburdened and poorly trained in spirituality, avoid or shut down deeper conversations (fear, guilt, questions about God and the meaning of life), reducing the patient to a “clinical case” without genuine attention to their existential needs.

* M. Balboni et al., “Unmet spiritual needs in palliative care: Psychometrics of a screening tool and prevalence in an international sample,” Palliative and Supportive Care, 2023. The study shows a high prevalence of unrecognized and unaddressed spiritual needs among patients in palliative care; E. Kroenke et al., “Loneliness of oncology patients at the end of life,” Supportive Care in Cancer, 2016; and J. Strömbom et al., “Loneliness at end-of-life: A scoping review,” Journal of Clinical Nursing, 2021. The authors document how loneliness and isolation in advanced cancer patients are associated with greater psychological distress and poorer quality of life; B. Puchalski et al., “Spiritual Care in the Global Sphere,” Journal of Palliative Medicine, 2020; and “Spirituality and palliative care: international models and new perspectives,” Current Opinion in Supportive and Palliative Care, 2025. The studies show that, despite formal recognition of spirituality in guidelines, there is often a lack of trained personnel and structured spiritual care programs, with the consequent risk of neglecting spiritual and existential needs.

Society has a duty to promote personalized relationships and communication, preventing the social and familial isolation of the elderly.

title: Charter, Art. 12 — The right to companionship and human connection (part 3)
title_en: Charter, Art. 12 — The right to companionship and human connection (part 3)
text:
Charter, Art. 12 — The right to companionship and human connection

This section on the elderly person at the threshold of the end of life reverses a perspective: at the center is not “the clinical case” but a person who, until the very last moment, remains a subject of relationships, care, and decision-making, to be rescued from the culture of discarding and abandonment. The entire Title V could be read as a legal-civil translation of that “culture of accompaniment” which I propose as the only alternative to both euthanasia and aggressive medical treatment.

The true Christian and civil response to end-of-life care is not medicalized solitude, but a presence that accompanies: “no” to abandonment, “no” to excessive treatment, “yes” to an accompaniment that moves the heart and remains by one’s side until the end. Article 12, with the right to be accompanied, listened to, and supported, and with the social duty to avoid isolation, takes up almost literally this culture of accompaniment as a public duty, not merely as a private or pastoral virtue.

title: Charter, Art. 13 — The right to palliative care, pain management, and relief from suffering (part 1)
title_en: Charter, Art. 13 — The right to palliative care, pain management, and relief from suffering (part 1)
text:
Charter, Art. 13 — The right to palliative care, pain management, and relief from suffering

Palliative care is defined by the World Health Organization as “a form of active and comprehensive care for people of all ages experiencing significant suffering related to a serious illness, with the aim of improving the quality of life of the patient, the family, and caregivers through the prevention and relief of physical, psychological, social, and spiritual suffering, without either hastening or delaying death.”*

A “palliative culture” must be promoted that stands in opposition to the throwaway culture: a service to life and the dignity of the person, not a technical preparation for death.5, 6Palliative care, initiated as soon as an incurable disease is diagnosed, must be strengthened and never dismantled, while also clarifying the clear distinction between palliative sedation (a therapeutic act to alleviate suffering) and euthanasia

* World Health Organization, Palliative Care. Fact Sheet, Geneva, WHO, 2020; Worldwide Hospice Palliative Care Alliance – World Health Organization, Global Atlas of Palliative Care, 2nd ed., London-Geneva, WHPC-WHO, 2020.

(an act intended to intentionally cause death). Article 14, which asserts the right to access the best pain management therapies “until the end” and calls for professionalism, humanity, and continuity of care, translates into a legal right what I have always described as the duty of a “humane and civilized” society toward those who “cannot manage on their own.”8

Globally, palliative care remains underdeveloped due to a combination of structural, cultural, political, and economic factors, despite being recognized as an essential component of universal health coverage.

Lack of policies and integration into healthcare systems

In many countries, palliative care is not clearly incorporated into national health policies, health plans, or basic service packages; therefore, it is neither funded nor systematically organized. Even where guidelines or official documents exist, palliative care is often not integrated into essential levels of care, in the community or in hospitals, remaining an isolated activity or dependent on external projects and donors.

Insufficient resources and global inequalities

The “Global Atlas of Palliative Care” shows that most advanced services are concentrated in North America, Europe, and Australia, while approximately 76% of the need is in low- and

middle-income countries. Many countries lack dedicated facilities, trained staff, essential medications, and home care systems; only about 14% of people worldwide who need palliative care actually receive it.

Limited access to opioids and regulatory barriers

Access to opioid analgesics, which are essential for managing severe pain, is very limited in much of the world due to restrictive regulations, complex bureaucracy, fear of “diversion,” and stigma surrounding the use of morphine.
