Charter, Art. 13 — The right to palliative care, pain management, and relief from suffering

In some countries, the procedures for prescribing and obtaining opioids are so complicated (special forms, specialized pharmacies, registrations) that they discourage doctors and families, leaving many patients with uncontrolled pain.

Lack of awareness and training*

Many policymakers and professionals do not fully understand what palliative care is, the con-

Kroenke et al., “Loneliness of oncology patients at the end of life,” Supportive Care in Cancer, 2016; J. Strömbom et al., “Loneliness at end-of-life: A scoping review,” Journal of Clinical Nursing, 2021; M. Miaskowski et al., “Loneliness and Symptom Burden in Oncology Patients,” Supportive Care in Cancer, 2021, which show how loneliness and isolation among advanced cancer patients are associated with greater psychological distress, more severe symptoms, and poorer quality of life; C.M. Puchalski et al., “Spiritual Care in the Global Sphere,” Journal of Palliative Medicine, 2020; and “Spirituality and palliative care: international models and new perspectives,” Current Opinion in Supportive and Palliative Care, 2025.

confuse them with “end-of-life care” or view them as an optional luxury rather than a necessary component of care.

In many countries, medical and nursing curricula devote little attention to palliative care, leaving clinicians feeling ill-prepared to manage pain, complex symptoms, and psycho-spiritual needs, and leading them to refer patients to specialist services infrequently or too late.

Older adults have the right to access palliative care and the best therapies for pain management, without cultural or economic barriers, in accordance with the principles of preserving dignity and controlling pain and suffering—whether physical, mental, or psychological—until the end of life.

Healthcare providers and the state have a duty to ensure professionalism, humanity, and continuity of care, so that it is always possible to provide care even when a cure is not possible.

title: Charter, Art. 14 — The Right to Proportionality of Treatment (part 1)
title_en: Charter, Art. 14 — The Right to Proportionality of Treatment (part 1)
text:
Charter, Art. 14 — The Right to Proportionality of Treatment

The elderly person must be able to receive treatments proportionate to their situation. Any futile medical treatment and the arbitrary suspension of care that serves their overall well-being are prohibited.

Society must support a shared assessment of the clinical appropriateness and personal value of treatments, involving the elderly person and their loved ones in the decision-making process.

The Pontifical Academy for Life has published a “Short Glossary on End-of-Life Care” in which it reaffirms a threefold “no”: to euthanasia, to assisted suicide, and to excessive medical treatment that prolongs suffering without real benefit to the person. The proportionality of treatments, with the prohibition of both excessive treatment and the arbitrary suspension of care beneficial to overall well-being, corresponds exactly

the distinction made by the Pontifical Academy for Life: it is permissible to suspend disproportionate measures, not because one desires death, but because one recognizes that “not activating disproportionate measures is equivalent to avoiding excessive medical treatment.”4 The call for a shared assessment between clinical and personal values regarding treatment reflects the idea, very dear to me, that the decision regarding end-of-life care is not an isolated technical act, but a communal discernment involving the patient, family, medical team, and, often, the broader community.

Thanks to the continuous innovation of knowledge and technologies, medicine certainly renders an enormous service, defeating diseases and helping to increase life expectancy. But if technocratic logic becomes prevalent, even the human body risks being interpreted and managed as a collection of organs to be repaired or replaced. As the Encyclical Laudato si’ states regarding technoscience, it is increasingly “difficult to use its resources without being dominated by its logic” (no. 108), that is, without being driven toward “a reductionism that affects human life and society in all their dimensions” (no. 107).

The criterion of proportionality is proposed as a reference point for modulating interventions (diagnostic and therapeutic) that are effectively at the service of the “integral good” indicated by Pope Francis. It lies at the point of convergence between two orders

of factors, both necessary for evaluating the treatments to be administered. On the first side are healthcare professionals, with their professional expertise. Physicians possess the knowledge to assess the clinical appropriateness of treatments for the current condition, considering their specific characteristics (availability, complexity of use, costs, risks) in relation to the expected benefits in terms of the patient’s health and well-being.

title: Charter, Art. 14 — The Right to Proportionality of Treatment (part 2)
title_en: Charter, Art. 14 — The Right to Proportionality of Treatment (part 2)
text:
Charter, Art. 14 — The Right to Proportionality of Treatment

However, these aspects are not sufficient to make a judgment of proportionality: a second set of factors must also be considered, concerning the burden and sustainability of the recommended interventions for the patient. Now, only the patient can assess the physical and mental strength they believe they possess, including based on their own values. Therefore, a judgment of proportionality cannot be made without the patient’s involvement. The patient has the final say regarding their own health and medical interventions on their own body:

“Decisions must be made by the patient, if he or she has the competence and capacity to do so, or, otherwise, by those who have the legal right to do so, always respecting the reasonable will and legitimate interests of the patient” (CCC, no. 2278). If this does not occur, the person is no longer recognized as the subject of care but reduced to an object to be disposed of.

title_en: Charter, Art. 15 — The right to shared care planning and advance healthcare directives (part 1)
text:
Charter, Art. 15 — The right to shared care planning and advance healthcare directives

The right to shared care planning (Advance Care Planning, ACP) and advance directives is by no means practiced uniformly and comprehensively worldwide, despite being recommended by international guidelines and many national health systems.

Right to shared care planning*

There is no universal implementation: review studies on ACP show that, even in high-income countries, only a minority of

* Brøderud L. et al., “Barriers and facilitators to the implementation of advance care planning: a multi-level perspective,” Frontiers in Health Services, 2025; Jimenez G. et al., “Barriers and facilitators to implementing advance care planning in healthcare: an explanatory systematic review of implementation studies,” Palliative Medicine, 2023; Rhee J. et al., “Why are advance care planning decisions not implemented?”, Palliative and Supportive Care, 2013; Sudore R.L., Lum H.D. et al., “Advance Care Planning and End-of-Life Communications”, NIH/StatPearls and related reviews, 2020–2023.

Few people have a shared care plan or a formalized advance directive; actual coverage varies widely across countries, regions, and social groups. At the international level, there are significant differences in the legal recognition of advance directives, the infrastructure for recording them, and the ability to access them easily at the appropriate clinical moment.

Cultural and individual barriers: Discussing advanced illness, death, and treatment limits is often a cultural or family taboo; many people prefer “not to know” or delegate completely to doctors, which makes it difficult to introduce shared advance planning in a timely manner. Patients and families may not fully understand the significance of advance directives, fear that

“signing something” will lead to receiving less care, or feel it is too early until the disease is very advanced.

Professional and organizational barriers: many healthcare providers report time constraints, heavy workloads, and a highly

“productivity-driven” organizational culture that prioritizes acute care and procedures over complex conversations about values, care goals, and end-of-life issues. Specific training, tools, and structured pathways for ACP are often lacking; these conversations are left to the goodwill of individual professionals rather than being integrated into mandatory protocols and clinical pathways.

Legal and systemic barriers: advance directives, where they exist, may have unclear legal status, differ from one legal system to another, or not be easily accessible in the medical record, making it difficult for caregivers to follow them in practice. Some healthcare settings lack electronic registries or a single source of truth where shared preferences and plans can be stored and quickly retrieved; consequently, even when planning is done, it is not implemented.

title: Charter, Art. 15 — The right to shared care planning and advance healthcare directives (part 2)
title_en: Charter, Art. 15 — The right to shared care planning and advance healthcare directives (part 2)
text:
Charter, Art. 15 — The right to shared care planning and advance healthcare directives

1J.1. Older adults have the right to plan their treatment path in advance, in dialogue with caregivers and family members, and to express preferences regarding end-of-life choices.

Ideological conflicts regarding advance directives and end-of-life care must be overcome to build shared planning pathways that help people express their preferences early on, through dialogue. Article 16, which recognizes the right to plan ahead, to engage in dialogue with healthcare providers and family members, and to use clear and transparent legal tools, is in line with the need for a “rule beyond ideologies”: no to solitary decision-making, no to oversimplifications, yes to tools that make it possible to support the patient’s freedom until the end.

1J.2. Society must promote legal tools, transparent procedures, and support for the drafting and observance of advance healthcare directives.

title: Charter, Art. 16 — The Right to Spiritual Care (part 1)
title_en: Charter, Art. 16 — The Right to Spiritual Care (part 1)
text:
Charter, Art. 16 — The Right to Spiritual Care

1.1. Older adults have the right to receive spiritual and religious support in accordance with their faith and sensibilities, in both public and private institutions.

The spiritual dimension is not an accessory to the confessional, but a constitutive part of holistic care: the person is body, mind, and spirit, and at the end of life questions of meaning, forgiveness, reconciliation, and hope emerge.20Article 17, which guarantees spiritual support in accordance with one’s faith and sensibilities in both public and private facilities, legally articulates this conviction that accompaniment must include words, rituals, and listening—not merely therapy and procedures. From this perspective, the chaplain, the minister of worship, and the spiritual counselor are not “accessories,” but part of the extended team that cares for the person in their entirety.

1.2. Societies and institutions must ensure listening, respect, and access to spiritual care at the end of life.

The right to spiritual care is neither guaranteed nor effectively and uniformly practiced worldwide, even though its importance is now recognized in many international documents and in definitions of palliative care. In fact, the WHO explicitly includes spiritual suffering in the definition of palliative care, stating that it aims to alleviate physical, psychological, social, and spiritual suffering and is recognized as part of the right to health. Recent analyses of spirituality in palliative care show that many national and professional guidelines (e.g., the United Kingdom, some European and Anglo-Saxon systems) recommend the assessment and management of spiritual needs.

Spirituality is often recognized in theory but poorly integrated into practice: many services lack structured models of spiritual care, trained staff, or systematic procedures for assessing spiritual needs.

The literature speaks of a veritable “gap” between recognition and practice: spirituality remains marginal in health policies, global health programs, and professional training in most contexts.

Main barriers (where and why)*

Global public health context: global health is predominantly secular, focused on measurable outcomes, and wary of religious or spiritual language; for this reason, spiritual issues are often excluded from funding streams, indicators, and programs.

Lack of universal standards: a review of spiritual care guidelines shows that no universally adopted approach exists; policies are more developed in some systems (e.g., the United Kingdom, Australia, parts of Europe) while regulatory or operational gaps persist in many other regions, particularly in low- and middle-income countries.

Lack of skills and clear roles: providing spiritual care requires specific skills; several reviews highlight that practitioners report insecurity, a lack of training, and poorly defined roles for chaplains and spiritual caregivers, resulting in a limited provision of structured spiritual care.

title: Charter, Art. 17 — The right to dignity in dying (part 1)
title_en: Charter, Art. 17 — The right to dignity in dying (part 1)
text:
Charter, Art. 17 — The right to dignity in dying

Dying is part of life. And it is a moment that reveals the truth of a society: if frail elderly people are cast aside, the entire community is impoverished. Article 18, which prohibits all forms of abandonment, abuse, or discrimination and calls for the defense of the dignity of the elderly by avoiding futile medical interventions—that is, according to the “triple no” that I believe must be articulated: no to euthanasia, no to abandonment, no to futile medical treatment; yes to accompaniment and care that recognizes the value of life even when it is frail and dependent. The call for respect for the person and for emotional relationships reflects a sensitivity whereby the person is not defined by illness, but by a network of bonds that precedes and survives them.

Today, there is no uniform, globally practiced recognition of the “dignity of dying” as an effective right; rather, there are principles and declarations that speak of dignity, but their concrete implementation varies greatly across countries and healthcare systems.

Why the dignity of dying is not respected

The majority of people worldwide lack access to basic palliative care, adequate pain relief, and psychosocial and spiritual support: approximately 14% of those who need it receive palliative care, with significant disparities between high-income countries and low- and middle-income countries.

In many regions (sub-Saharan Africa, parts of Asia, rural Latin America, and fragile areas of Eastern Europe), the end of life often occurs with uncontrolled pain, limited support, little information, and without shared planning processes—in clear contrast to the idea of a “dignified” death.

Main reasons for lack of implementation*

Palliative care as a “neglected priority”: palliative care, which is the primary practical tool for ensuring dignity at the end of life, remains underdeveloped and underfunded, despite the 2014 WHA Resolution 67. calling for its universal integration.

Harding R. et al., “Confronting global inequities in palliative care,” BMJ Global Health, 2025, which shows how severe inequalities in access to palliative care result in millions of deaths involving avoidable suffering, in contrast to any notion of a dignified death; United Nations/ECLAC, The Right to End-of-Life Palliative Care and a Dignified Death, which analyzes the legal recognition of the right to a dignified death in certain Latin American countries and the gaps in its implementation; Sulmasy D., “The Concept of Dignity and Its Use in End-of-Life Debates,” which examines how the notion of dignity is interpreted differently in various national contexts, with consequences for end-of-life policies and practices; Peeler A., Afolabi O., Harding R., “Palliative care is an overlooked global health priority,” BMJ, 2024, which describes palliative care as a neglected priority and directly links the lack of palliative care to a loss of dignity in dying.

title: Charter, Art. 17 — The right to dignity in dying (part 2)
title_en: Charter, Art. 17 — The right to dignity in dying (part 2)
text:
Charter, Art. 17 — The right to dignity in dying

Differences in the interpretation of dignity: comparative studies (e.g., on England and France) show that “dignity” can be interpreted as the primacy of individual autonomy or as a duty to protect the vulnerable; this leads to very different laws and practices regarding sedation, withdrawal of treatment, and euthanasia/assisted dying.

Taboos surrounding death and end-of-life care: in many contexts, discussing death, end-of-life decisions, and advance directives is culturally difficult; this hinders structured processes that would enable the effective respect for dignity in dying.

Euthanasia

The term “euthanasia,” meaning “gentle death,” was already used by Francis Bacon in 1605 to refer to care for the dying person, intended to provide relief during the final stage of life. But since the late 19th century, the term has come to be used to refer to the death of a patient caused “out of mercy.” And this is the meaning that has taken hold in current discussions in various parts of the world, with countries that have legalized and regulated this practice.

In the international ethical-legal context, euthanasia generally refers to the act by which a physician or other healthcare professional intentionally causes the death of a person, at their explicit and informed request, with the aim of ending

suffering deemed unbearable and otherwise unalleviable.

Recurring elements in international definitions:

the intervention is intentional (causing death is the direct purpose, not a side effect);

the person is competent and consenting, and makes a clear and repeated request;

the stated purpose is to alleviate severe suffering associated with an incurable disease or irreversible clinical condition.

In the encyclical Evangelium Vitae, however, a broader definition of euthanasia is given, referring to “an action or omission which, by its nature and in its intentions, procures death, with the aim of eliminating all pain” (John Paul II 1995, n. 65). This avoids any qualifying adjectives used to distinguish various types of euthanasia, such as “active” or “passive.” The former referred to an act that causes death by administering lethal drugs (killing). The second, on the other hand, referred to the omission of an intervention that prevents death and allows the pathological process to run its course, either by not initiating therapy or by suspending it once it has begun (letting die). The confusion arises from the fact that the administration of lethal drugs is always euthanasia, whereas letting die may be euthanasia, but not necessarily. It would in fact be euthanasia to omit or suspend effective, appropriate, and sustainable treatment on the part of the patient. It would instead be le-

legitimate, indeed a duty, to terminate treatment (including life-sustaining treatment) that is deemed disproportionate.

title: Charter, Art. 17 — The right to dignity in dying (part 3)
title_en: Charter, Art. 17 — The right to dignity in dying (part 3)
text:
Charter, Art. 17 — The right to dignity in dying

Speaking of disproportionate treatments. The therapeutic possibilities of medicine have grown significantly in recent decades, enabling the cure and prevention of many diseases and making more effective treatments available. While these successes are undoubtedly commendable, there is also a need to reaffirm the

“centrality” of the patient, with a personalized approach that allows for the definition of effective and appropriate care for each individual patient. Especially when the clinical situation worsens, the therapies used are no longer capable of achieving a cure, and the patient is moving toward the terminal phase of life, the question arises: how much should we persist? At what point should we stop? When should certain treatments not be initiated?

These are the questions that arise for many cancer patients or those with neurodegenerative diseases, for whom the term “therapeutic overzealousness” is commonly used. Generally, however, the term “disproportionate use of treatments” is preferred, defined as the persistence in continuing or initiating medical treatments that are disproportionate to the goals of care, useless or ineffective in altering the prognosis or improving quality of life, and such as to impose on the patient serious burdens, risks, or suffering without a reasonably expected benefit.

Other Forms of Euthanasia

In many contexts, ageism and the undertreatment of the elderly constitute a genuine form of therapeutic neglect: advanced age effectively becomes a criterion for reduced clinical investment and a diminished provision of palliative and rehabilitative care. Although this is not euthanasia in the technical-legal sense, this systematic refusal to provide care can be interpreted as a disguised form of cultural euthanasia, which shortens life or increases suffering for reasons of age rather than based on proportionate clinical assessments. It then becomes even more important to provide support: this is the point on which we can all agree, beyond differing positions on terms, strategies, and approaches. If we start from the simple, fundamental, and—I firmly believe—widely shared need to support and not abandon the elderly person grappling with end-of-life issues, the complexity unravels along the thread of Ariadne’s in a strategy of closeness: human, spiritual, and systemic.

Reviews of ageism in healthcare show that older adults often receive lower-quality care, with delayed diagnoses, reduced access to standard treatments, and greater barriers to using services, leading to “non-care and neglect.”

In geriatric oncology, for example, older adults are less likely to receive therapies considered standard or potentially curative compared to patients

with the same clinical condition; this leads to higher mortality linked to undertreatment, not overtreatment.

title: Charter, Art. 17 — The right to dignity in dying (part 4)
title_en: Charter, Art. 17 — The right to dignity in dying (part 4)
text:
Charter, Art. 17 — The right to dignity in dying

Studies on inequalities in palliative care document that older adults receive poorer symptom management, less access to specialized palliative care, and less involvement in decision-making compared to younger patients.

Therapeutic neglect thus becomes a consequence of ageism. Age is used as an implicit criterion to deem an older adult “less deserving” of diagnostic tests, intensive care, rehabilitation, or disease-modifying treatments. Various symptoms and problems (“he’s unwell,” “he’s confused,” “he can’t walk anymore”) are often dismissed as “normal aging,” without adequate assessment or management. This results in the aforementioned systematic undertreatment—that is, a level of care below actual need—effectively a form of neglect, even if not explicitly labeled as such in scientific literature.

There is, therefore, a structural risk of therapeutic neglect:

due to access limitations (poor or unequal systems);

due to explicit or implicit ageism;

due to the absence of well-integrated geriatric and palliative care models.

It is a form of “implicit euthanasia,” an informal euthanasia-like attitude (“he’s so old anyway…”

old”), which is reflected in three documented phenomena:

undertreatment of “fit” older adults (who could tolerate and benefit from active care), who receive fewer standard treatments than younger people;

limited access to palliative and concurrent care, especially among the very elderly, who are left without either adequate therapy or true comprehensive care;

decisions to limit life-sustaining treatments (withholding/withdrawal) that vary widely across countries, hospitals, and individual physicians, with the risk that choices are influenced more by culture and prejudice than by transparent clinical criteria.

The elderly person must be recognized as a person of value until the very end.

No form of neglect, discrimination, or physical or psychological abuse can be tolerated.

Society and the healthcare system are called upon to defend the dignity of the elderly, to avoid all unnecessary medical intervention, and to promote respect for the individual and their emotional relationships.

title: Charter, Art. 18 — The Right to Choose Post-Mortem Practices
title_en: Charter, Art. 18 — The Right to Choose Post-Mortem Practices
text:
Charter, Art. 18 — The Right to Choose Post-Mortem Practices

18.1. Older adults have the right to express their own wishes regarding cremation, burial, organ donation, and the disposition of their bodies, which society must respect and protect.

It is appropriate for the person to decide on their own cremation, burial, organ donation, and the disposition of their body, as an expression of the fact that responsibility and personal history do not end with the last breath. We must insist on the dignity of the body and the sanctity of the person, in order to preserve the symbolic and relational value of dying and the afterlife: society is called to respect and protect these choices, recognizing that the elderly person retains a central role that continues beyond life.
